Certainly if you had canvassed the opinions of many seasoned Boro followers.

The Robins may have won just twice in their past 10 Championship matches – with head coach Michael Skubala starting to come under growing scrutiny – but the sight of the Teessiders seems to bring out the best in the West Country outfit.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

The red side of Bristol have won the last five of their last six league fixtures against Boro while drawing the other.

All told they have triumphed in 16 out of 28 league meetings in the 21st century, losing just six.

Kim Hellberg suffered his first defeat as Boro chief against City – who renew acquaintances with former loan goalkeeper and player-of-the-season Radek Vitek – last December in a 2-0 pre-Christmas defeat at Ashton Gate.

The reverse fixture on Teesside in March, a 1-1 draw, was far more damaging in the final analysis for Boro, who conceded a painful and needless stoppage-time equaliser at a critical juncture of the run-in when their automatic promotion credentials were placed into jeopardy.

In all competitions, the Robins have lost just once in 15 visits to the Riverside Stadium, winning on eight occasions.

Hellberg, whose high-flying side head into the game on the back of no wins – and no goals – in their past two games against Watford and Wrexham, said: "I know that sometimes things happen in football when you face a team you haven't beaten for a long time.

"Things like that happen; it's difficult to describe why. I think last season, we played some very good games against them and created a lot of opportunities and thought we maybe should have won both of them and came away with one point at the end.

Sources indicate that "We are trying to prepare for a team who have been very strong away from home and struggling at home. But they have been one of the best sides away from home and picking up points.

"It will be a tough game like always and hopefully we can win.".

After their international exertions with USA and Australia, midfielders Sebastian Berhalter and Riley McGree only returned to full training on Friday, when Jeremy Sarmiento was also due back following his commitments with Ecuador.

Billy Sharp has described Doncaster Rovers manager Grant McCann as “ruthless” - but does not hold any grudges regarding his departure.

The 40-year-old left Doncaster at the end of last season, signing off in style with a final-day hat-trick away at Peterborough United.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

He later hung up his boots, but did recently come out of retirement to play for AFC Rushden & Diamonds in the FA Cup.

Sharp had expressed interest in a coaching role at Sheffield United while still on Doncaster’s books and believes it had a factor in the decision to release him.

In a recent development, he told the DN4 Podcast: “I don’t hold any grudges at all. He’s a ruthless manager and you’ve got to make decisions. Sometimes you get decisions wrong. I’m sure it did have a part to play, I think so, but only he knows.

According to recent reports, “I think you have to be ruthless as a manager. I’m stubborn as well. If I ask myself, if I was manager and a player came to me... but I don’t know. It was different because I was coming to the end of my career, I’m a Sheffield United fan, I was trying to think about the future.

According to recent reports, “It wasn’t that I wasn’t enjoying training or playing. It had been arranged to retire. But I don’t know, I really wanted the opportunity. I thought it was a great opportunity for me to be in the game for the next 15, 20, whatever years.”.

Sharp has repeatedly expressed a desire to move into coaching and with his playing days now seemingly behind him, the iconic marksman can shift his focus.

Given the wealth of experience possessed by the Sheffield United legend and ex-Leeds United man, he would arguably be a shrewd addition to an array of coaching set-ups.

“Grant always remarked to me about doing a bit of coaching at Donny,” he said. “He obviously brought Greeny (Paul Green) up.

“When I was injured, towards the back end of the season, looking out of that physio room, wanting to be on that training pitch, I could see myself doing a bit of coaching as well.”.

  • Two teams at opposite ends of the Eredivisie table meet on Sunday as FC Twente welcome Willem II to De Grolsch Veste.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Adepoju Marvellous | 20 Nov 2026 15:36, Last updated: 20 Nov 2026 19:58.

Two teams at opposite ends of the Eredivisie table meet on Sunday as FC Twente welcome Willem II to De Grolsch Veste.

The hosts are aiming for a fourth consecutive win in this fixture to remain within touching distance of their title rivals, while the visitors are desperate for a victory to spark what has been an underwhelming campaign so far.

Twente’s 2-2 draw against Ajax just before the break saw their four-game winning run come to an end, but given they were 2-0 down midway through the second half, securing a share of the spoils resoundingly feels like a point earned rather than two lost.

Sources indicate that just two points behind current leaders PSV Eindhoven, John van den Brom’s side remain firmly in the title race. While they trail Feyenoord, PSV, and Ajax in goals scored, they boast the league's best defence with just 12 goals conceded, and only Heerenveen have kept more clean sheets.

Industry observers note that three weeks after recording their largest-ever win - a 9-0 thrashing of SBV Excelsior - the Tukkers have a chance to lay down another marker against the division’s bottom club. Given rising expectations, a victory here feels almost non-negotiable.

On a personal note, Van den Brom will also want to preserve his impressive record against this weekend’s opposite number; across their previous 11 meetings, the Twente boss has recorded seven wins and four draws.

After winning each of their first home league matches this term, Sunday’s hosts have collected just one point from their last two outings and now seek to avoid going three straight Eredivisie matches in Enschede without a win for the first time since April 2025.

Willem II ended a run of six consecutive league defeats with a 1-1 draw against PEC Zwolle on November 6, but their wait for a first victory continues, as the appointment of Jurgen Streppel has yet to yield the desired turnaround.

Recent findings suggest that streppel returned for a second spell to replace John Stegeman, who managed just two points from a possible 27 over nine matches. The Zwolle stalemate was only Willem II's third point of the season, at least six fewer than any other team.

Already 12 points worse off than at this stage of their 2024-25 relegation campaign, De Superkruiken face a herculean task to avoid the drop. Upcoming fixtures against Twente and Feyenoord - two of the current top four - over the next three gameweeks only add to their challenge.

A league-high 40 goals conceded means Willem II are frequently punished for their league-low 11 goals scored. Consequently, there must be drastic improvement at one end of the pitch if they are to turn things around.

Facing a team that have scored 14 goals in the final 30 minutes of matches, Sunday’s hosts cannot afford to lose focus in a period in which they have conceded 19 goals, just under half of their season total.

FC Twente form (all competitions):.

Willem II form (all competitions):.

Max Bruns has not featured for Twente since September and remains unavailable, one of two defenders out of contention alongside Stav Lemkin, with the Israeli international suffering a long-term injury just before the start of the season.

Twenty-year-old Filip Erik Thorvaldsen is set to miss a sixth consecutive game for the hosts, who are also still without first-choice goalkeeper Lars Unnerstall.

Wout Weghorst is one of four players tied on nine goals in the Golden Boot race, and the striker will be eager to add to his tally.

Justin Hoogma (knee) and Amine Lachkar (groin) are Willem II’s two guaranteed absentees for Sunday’s clash, with the latter sidelined since July 2025.

However, French shot-stopper Thomas Didillon could also miss out for the away side, having featured just once since mid-August.

FC Twente possible starting lineup:.

Drommel; Van Rooy, Propper, Nijstad, Adelgaard; Zerrouki, Weidmann; Rots, Taha, Orjasaeter; Weghorst.

Willem II possible starting lineup:.

Delanghe; Tjoe-A-On, Dekker, Stam, Ter Avest; Twigt, Zarrouk; Van Crooy, Van Aalst, Vilhena; Haen.

On paper, Sunday’s fixture appears to be Twente’s easiest game of the season so far, but as has been seen on several occasions, things are rarely that straightforward.

Still, we fully expect the hosts to make light work of their visitors and cruise to all three points at the end of 90 minutes.

Chelsea will have to do without a trio of key players when they host Leeds United tomorrow (November 21).

The old rivals will meet again at Stamford Bridge having done battle in the Carabao Cup in August. Leeds will be out to avenge their 6-3 loss, while Chelsea will be keen to break into the Premier League’s top four with a victory.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Many will fancy Chelsea to claim three points but the Blues will not be at full strength when Daniel Farke’s side visit.

Influential forward Joao Pedro is the headline absentee, with the 25-year-old yet to return to training after picking up a thigh problem.

Alonso remarked: “He’s not yet fit to train with the team. We need to wait a bit more. He’s not going to be available for Leeds. We need to see day by day how he is feeling.”.

Alongside the Brazilian on the absentee list is defender Maxence Lacroix, who is a hamstring problem and is in a “similar situation” to Pedro.

There will also be no place in the squad for Netherlands international defender Jorrel Hato, who has a back injury.

Alonso said: “Jorrel has a back problem. We need to be patient because it’s going to take a while.”.

Recent findings suggest that chelsea will, however, be able to start Moises Caicedo despite the midfielder’s withdrawal at half-time in a recent friendly for Ecuador. Defender Josh Acheampong is also fit and available to face the Whites, as is goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez.

According to recent reports, regarding the latter, Alonso said: “He is in the squad and he is selectable. Against Sunderland two weeks ago probably there was risk, and the proposal was for him to train more with Argentina and to play one game. It went well so he’s available for tomorrow.”.

Chelsea have not yet welcomed defender Reece James back to action and although they have brought winger Jamie Gittens back in, he requires time to reach full fitness.

Alonso noted: “Reece is getting there. He’s taking a step forward, but still needs some weeks.

“Jamie Gittens is better. He’s already training with the team, but we want to give him more time until he comes back in the squad.”.

Structural and regulatory evolution across the genus Hordeum

💡 Key Takeaways

  • To maximize phylogenetic representation across the genus, we selected 27 accessions representing 24 Hordeum species, encompassing all recognized diploid genome groups1 together with representative tetraploid and hexaploid lineages (Extended Data Fig.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The genus Hordeum comprises cultivated barley and its wild relatives, an evolutionarily, ecologically and agriculturally crucial group of grasses1,2. Here we generated a chromosome-scale comparative genomic resource comprising all recognized diploid Hordeum species together with representative polyploid lineages. Comparative analyses reveal extensive structural variation, including inversions and chromosomal rearrangements that disrupt proximal collinearity and reflect lineage-specific genome remodelling. Single-copy gene phylogenies identify ancient hybridization, segmental exchange and introgression, revealing pervasive reticulate evolution during Hordeum diversification. We uncover widespread horizontal gene transfer from Panicoideae grasses into Hordeum, with many transferred genes showing evidence of transcription and functional integration. Retrotransposon proliferation explains genome size variation and provides insights into polyploid genome evolution. Whole-genome alignments reveal contrasting evolutionary dynamics: whereas coding sequences remain highly conserved, regulatory elements undergo rapid turnover, providing a rich source of regulatory diversity for phenotypic evolution. Case studies of vernalization and glume development demonstrate how natural variation in regulatory and coding sequences contributes to flowering time and floral morphology. This comprehensive pangenomic framework establishes Hordeum as a model for studying genome evolution, structural variation and the genetic basis of adaptive traits, offering fresh avenues for barley improvement.

According to recent reports, the genus Hordeum comprises approximately 33 species and is widely distributed across the temperate regions of Eurasia and the Americas1,2,3. Hordeum is classified into two subgenera based on cytogenetic evidence: one containing the H and Xu genomes and the other containing the I and Xa genomes4. The basic chromosome number is seven, and, although most species are diploid, tetraploid and hexaploid taxa have also been described. Cultivated barley (Hordeum vulgare) is the best known and most extensively studied species, as it represents one of the earliest domesticated cereal crops. Today, barley is the world’s fourth most notable grain, valued for its use in food, animal feed and brewing5. Cultivated barley and its wild progenitor (H. vulgare subsp. spontaneum) constitute a single inter-fertile gene pool, allowing for frequent gene flow between wild and cultivated forms6. This primary gene pool has long been exploited by breeders to introduce desirable traits6. Hordeum bulbosum has contributed valuable disease resistance genes through introgression7,8,9,10 due to its ability to hybridize directly with cultivated barley. The other Hordeum species are not domesticated but have important ecological and agricultural roles in ecosystem stability, environmental adaptation and forage use11,12,13,14,15. Together, Hordeum is both an agronomically important genus and a powerful model for studying crop evolution, environmental adaptation and resistance to biotic and abiotic stresses. Factors such as incomplete lineage sorting, recurrent hybridization and gene flow partly obscure species boundaries, leaving major evolutionary questions unresolved1,2,4,16,17. Recent barley pangenomes have substantially advanced our understanding of genomic variation within cultivated barley and its closest relatives10,18,19. However, these studies were largely confined to two species (H. vulgare and H. bulbosum) and therefore could not resolve genome-wide evolutionary processes operating across the genus, including the origin of large-scale structural variation, ancient hybridization, polyploid genome evolution and the diversification of regulatory loci. Extending comparative genomic analyses to encompass the entire genus is therefore essential to capture the full breadth of diversity within the Hordeum gene pool and to facilitate both evolutionary studies and the effective utilization of wild germplasm for barley improvement. Pangenomics now offers comprehensive resources to address such complexity. In crops such as tomato, potato, maize, grapevine, citrus and cotton, genus-level pangenomes have uncovered extensive structural variations, gene presence–absence and evolutionary dynamics20,21,22,23,24. Investigating structural variations helps to explain evolutionary processes and can inform crop breeding strategies25. However, the full extent of structural variation within Hordeum remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we generated chromosome-scale genome assemblies representing all recognized diploid Hordeum species together with representative polyploid lineages. This comparative genomic framework provides a view of structural and regulatory genome evolution across the genus, yielding latest insights into genome evolution and establishing a foundation for the utilization of wild diversity in barley improvement.

To maximize phylogenetic representation across the genus, we selected 27 accessions representing 24 Hordeum species, encompassing all recognized diploid genome groups1 together with representative tetraploid and hexaploid lineages (Extended Data Fig. 1a, Supplementary Table 1 and Supplementary Figs. 1–25). The dataset comprises 22 diploid accessions, 4 tetraploid accessions and 1 hexaploid accession. Twenty-four genome sequences were assembled using PacBio HiFi accurate long reads and Hi-C data (Supplementary Tables 2 and 3 and Supplementary Figs. 26–28), using the TRITEX pipeline26,27. The sequence assemblies of H. vulgare and H. bulbosum were sourced from our previous work10,28. The previously published chromosome-level assembly of Hordeum marinum H559 (ref. 29) was updated using the TRITEX pipeline, and previously published transcriptome data, Bionano optical maps and Hi-C data of Hordeum erectifolium NGB6816 were used30. The average contig N50 of the assemblies is 39.24 Mb. Assembly sizes range from 2.90 Gb to 4.48 Gb (mean, 3.92 Gb) in diploid species and from 7.49 Gb to 8.56 Gb (mean, 8.16 Gb) in tetraploid species, whereas the single hexaploid genome has an assembly size of 10.90 Gb. Chloroplast genome assemblies range from 136,335 bp to 137,079 bp (mean, 136,840 bp) (Supplementary Table 1). High assembly quality is supported by an average long terminal repeat (LTR) assembly index (LAI) of 14.79, a consensus quality value (QV) of 67.30 and k-mer completeness of 97.22% (Supplementary Table 4). For the heterozygous diploid species H. bulbosum, the two phased haplotypes were designated as Hap1 and Hap2. For polyploid species, independently assembled chromosome sets derived from different ancestral genomes were defined as subgenomes and denoted as Sub1, Sub2 and Sub3 according to their phylogenetic relationships with diploid progenitor lineages (Fig. 1a). To assess the gene content in the Hordeum pangenome, we annotated all genomes using transcriptome data (Methods and Supplementary Tables 5 and 6). A gene consolidation method was applied to ensure high comparability of gene predictions, including those for Hordeum parodii (6x) and Hordeum gussoneanum (4x). The number of high-confidence gene models identified ranges from 35,573 for diploid Hordeum murinum to 94,943 for hexaploid H. parodii (Supplementary Table 7). We assessed the quality of the Hordeum gene annotations using BUSCO (v5.8.0) with the poales_odb12 dataset, comprising 6,282 near-universal single-copy orthologues from Poales. On average, 97.35% of BUSCO genes were identified as complete, 0.69% as fragmented and 1.84% as missing (Supplementary Table 7). Independent benchmarking with OMArk and PSAURON further confirmed the high completeness and overall quality of the gene annotations (Supplementary Table 7). Transposable element (TE) annotation using the panEDTA pipeline31 revealed that transposons constituted on average 86.12% of the genome, ranging from 83.27% to 90.35% (Supplementary Table 8).

According to recent reports, based on the annotated gene sets of all species, we constructed a gene-based Hordeum pangenome. Overall, 42.4% of genes were classified as core genes, 56.5% as shell genes and 1.1% as cloud genes (Extended Data Fig. 1b,c). Gene ontology enrichment analysis indicated that phosphorylation- and kinase-related functions were enriched among core genes, ATP and RNA binding were enriched among shell genes, and defence response and oxidative stress response were enriched among cloud genes (Supplementary Fig. 29). Nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat (NLR) genes are key components of the plant immune system and have essential roles in resistance to fungal and other pathogens32,33. A map of their diversity is critical for advancing our understanding of disease resistance mechanisms in crops. Analysis of NLR genes revealed that I genome species contain significantly more NLR genes than the other Hordeum genome groups (Welch’s t-test, P = 1.8 × 10−6) (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b). To further characterize this diversity, we constructed an NLR pangenome across Hordeum haploid genome equivalents (haplomes), comprising 800 orthogroups, of which 13.75% were classified as core, 27.75% as shell and 58.50% as cloud gene families (Extended Data Fig. 2c). In addition, NLR gene clusters were significantly less abundant on chromosomes 4H and 5H than on the remaining chromosomes (Wilcoxon test, P < 2.2 × 10−16) (Extended Data Fig. 2d). Similarly, genome-wide analyses of pentatricopeptide repeat (PPR) proteins and mitochondrial transcription termination factors (mTERFs) revealed significant expansions of restorer-of-fertility-like (RFL) subgroups in the I and Xa genome groups relative to the H and Xu genome groups. Because RFL proteins are involved in fertility restoration in plants carrying cytoplasmic male sterility (CMS)34, these expansions suggest that the smaller RFL repertoires of the H and Xu genome groups are derived rather than ancestral (Supplementary Fig. 30a–e and Supplementary Table 9). Expansion of RFL-PPRs was most pronounced in the I genome group, whereas RFL-mTERFs were significantly expanded in both the I and Xa genome groups. Notably, RFL-mTERF genes clustered on the short arm of chromosome 6H exhibited extensive copy-number variation between Xa–I and H–Xu genome groups (t-test, P = 5.2 × 10−6) (Supplementary Fig. 30f). This region includes the Rfm3 locus, which partially restores fertility in plants carrying the msm1 cytoplasm used in hybrid barley breeding35 (Supplementary Fig. 30g).

To assess the feasibility of graph-based pangenome analyses across highly diverged Hordeum genomes, we constructed a pangenome graph using Progressive Cactus and hal2vg, comprising 2.53 billion nodes and 3.46 billion edges (68.7 Gb). Approximately 68% of nodes represented single-base variants, illustrating the extensive sequence divergence captured by the graph. Although computationally intensive tasks such as indexing remained infeasible (Methods), we successfully performed global analyses of core, shell and cloud sequence content, graph saturation, sequence conservation and variant diversity (Supplementary Figs. 31–34). These results demonstrate both the potential of graph-based approaches for genus-wide comparative genomics and the need for more scalable methods for graph exploration and interpretation.

Previous studies have inferred the evolutionary relationships among Hordeum species from plastome and partial gene sequences1,17. However, the relationships among some species remained weakly supported. In this study, we reconstructed a maximum-likelihood tree using a genome-wide single-copy gene set. Unlike previous phylogenies1,17, our species tree resolved all major evolutionary relationships with maximum bootstrap support, particularly among the recently diverged I-genome species (Supplementary Fig. 35). To further evaluate the robustness of these relationships, we reconstructed an independent coalescent-based species tree using ASTRAL-Pro3 (Supplementary Fig. 36), which integrates individual maximum-likelihood gene trees, and a genome-wide phylogeny inferred by CASTER from whole-genome multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) (Supplementary Figs. 37 and 38). We also estimated the divergence times of these species using fourfold degenerate third-codon transversion (4DTV) sites, excluding genomic regions identified as putatively derived from ancient hybridization (Supplementary Table 13). We estimated the divergence time between H and Xu at 10.3 million years ago (Ma), whereas I and Xa diverged around 9 Ma. The crown-group age of Hordeum dates back approximately 12.27 Ma (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 10). The chromosomes of Triticeae species exhibit high collinearity at their distal chromosome regions36, which is also the case in Hordeum (Fig. 1b). However, when aligned, the proximal regions show substantial loss of collinearity and highly fragmented alignments. Whole-genome comparisons across Hordeum species revealed that chromosomal rearrangements accumulated progressively with evolutionary divergence, contributing to the loss of collinearity and increasingly fragmented alignments in proximal chromosomal regions (Fig.1c, Extended Data Fig. 3a, Supplementary Figs. 39–44 and Supplementary Table 11). Quantification of reverse-orientation alignments across all Hordeum haplomes further demonstrated that putative inversions accumulated significantly more rapidly in proximal than in distal chromosome regions during Hordeum evolution (Supplementary Fig. 45). Among the seven chromosomes, chromosome 4H exhibited the most extensive loss of proximal collinearity (Supplementary Table 12). Recently diverged species retained strong chromosome-scale collinearity despite the presence of numerous structural variants, whereas comparisons between the deeply diverged H–Xu and Xa–I genome groups (more than 9 Ma) revealed almost complete fragmentation of proximal collinearity (Fig. 1c, Extended Data Fig. 3a and Supplementary Figs. 39–44). To estimate the size of non-collinear regions, we applied normalized coverage to identify these regions in species that diverged more than 9 Ma (Extended Data Fig. 3c,d, Supplementary Figs. 46–50 and Methods). In total, we determined the genome-wide distribution of non-collinear regions across chromosomes in Hordeum, with a cumulative size of 855 Mb identified in the H. vulgare genome (Supplementary Table 12). Given the central role of TEs in genome evolution, we compared TE composition between proximal and distal chromosome regions. Proximal regions contained a significantly higher proportion of TEs than distal regions (one-sided paired Wilcoxon test, P = 9.31 × 10−10), primarily due to an increased abundance of LTR/Gypsy retrotransposons (one-sided paired Wilcoxon test, P = 9.31 × 10−10) (Extended Data Fig. 4a,b and Supplementary Fig. 51). Together with the accumulation of large chromosomal rearrangements, these observations motivated a ‘stretch and twist’ model describing two complementary processes underlying the progressive loss of collinearity. The stretch component represents alignment displacement caused by TE amplification, whereas the twist component represents large-scale chromosomal rearrangements driven by structural variation (Extended Data Fig. 4c).

Recent findings suggest that in contrast to the dynamic structural variations found in proximal regions, the distal regions displayed more conserved, shared structural variations. This highlights that the extensive loss of collinearity in proximal regions precludes reliable identification of structural variants across more distantly related Hordeum species. Notably, large structural variations in the distal regions were predominantly inversions. On chromosomes 3H and 7H, we identified two large inversions spanning nearly the entire chromosome and present in multiple species (Extended Data Fig. 4d). In total, 1,407 inversions larger than 2 Mb were identified across Hordeum species (Extended Data Fig. 4d). The construction of a comprehensive inversion map revealed six inversions on chromosome 1H that were unexpectedly shared across divergent phylogenetic lineages (Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 5). We hypothesized that these large-scale structural variations might have originated from introgression events involving extensive chromosomal segments. We constructed a phylogenetic tree using the single-copy gene set from these regions to test this hypothesis. The resulting tree, resolved with maximum bootstrap support, confirmed that these structural variations are shared between one clade of the I genome group and the H–Xu genome groups (Fig. 2b). Moreover, 10 extant diploid Hordeum species diversified within 1.68 million years following the inferred hybridization event, whereas no comparable radiation occurred in other phylogenetic lineages during the same period (Figs. 1a and 2b and Extended Data Fig. 5). Notably, the alternative phylogenetic topology extends across contiguous chromosomal regions of approximately 200 Mb rather than isolated loci, indicating the inheritance of chromosome-scale haplotypes that are more consistent with ancient introgression than with stochastic gene tree discordance or incomplete lineage sorting.

It has been revealed that to identify additional signatures of ancient hybridization across the genus, we developed a genome-wide scanning approach based on local phylogenetic discordance among single-copy genes. The single-copy gene set was partitioned into sliding windows, and normalized Robinson–Foulds (nRF) distance was calculated between local phylogenetic trees and the genome-wide species tree (Extended Data Fig. 6a). Peaks in nRF values indicate genomic regions with phylogenetic histories that deviate from the species tree and therefore represent candidate introgression events. Here, we define hybridization footprints as large chromosomal segments shared among multiple descendant species that consistently exhibit an alternative phylogenetic relationship relative to the genome-wide species tree. Using an empirical threshold of 0.21 derived from the genome-wide nRF distribution to distinguish discordance peaks from background variation (Extended Data Fig. 6b and Supplementary Fig. 52), we recovered the chromosome 1H hybridization signal, validating the genome-wide scanning approach. Additionally, we detected more than ten consecutive windows with strong phylogenetic discordance signals at multiple regions (Extended Data Fig. 6c and Supplementary Fig. 52). To further explore the underlying causes of these inconsistencies, we reconstructed local phylogenetic trees using the single-copy gene sets from these regions (Extended Data Fig. 6e,f, Supplementary Figs. 53–58 and Supplementary Table 13). Regions in which local phylogenies consistently supported a specific alternative relationship across a large chromosomal segment were interpreted as evidence of ancient hybridization. By comparing the regions that exhibited phylogenetic discordance with the whole-genome tree, we identified two large-scale segmental exchanges occurring within Hordeum jubatum, with maximum bootstrap support (Extended Data Fig. 6e,f and Supplementary Table 13). Surprisingly, this large-scale segmental exchange explains the major duplication and deletion pattern previously identified on chromosome 5H relative to the H. vulgare reference genome (Supplementary Figs. 12, 56, 59 and 60). The exchanged regions in the two H. jubatum subgenomes are each more closely related to different ancestral genomes, indicating that the apparent duplication and deletion resulted from ancestral segmental exchange rather than independent copy-number changes. (Extended Data Fig. 6d). In the allotetraploid H. gussoneanum, extensive segmental exchanges were detected between the two subgenomes on chromosomes 2, 5 and 7 (Extended Data Fig. 6e, Supplementary Figs. 53, 55 and 57 and Supplementary Table 13). In the allohexaploid H. parodii, subgenome 1 carried a large chromosomal segment on chromosome 7 derived from Hordeum stenostachys, whereas subgenomes 2 and 3 exhibited an additional segmental exchange on chromosome 4 (Extended Data Fig. 6f, Supplementary Figs. 54, 55 and 58 and Supplementary Table 13). Together, these megabase-scale structural variants preserve signatures of ancient interspecific hybridization and large-scale chromosomal exchange that are not evident from genome-wide phylogenies alone, providing newly introduced insights into the complex evolutionary history of Hordeum.

According to recent reports, genetic variation is essential for species evolution. Beyond sexual reproduction, horizontal gene transfer (HGT) serves as an evolutionary shortcut for acquiring novel genes. Traditionally considered rare in vascular plants, genomic advances have revealed widespread occurrences of HGT, challenging prior assumptions37,38. Our previous research demonstrated extensive HGT in Hordeum. Notably, species within section stenostachys (I genome; 16 out of 22 diploid species) possess ribosomal DNA (rDNA) acquired from grasses in the subfamily Panicoideae (for example, Panicum, Paspalum and Setaria)39,40. The oldest transfers (from Panicum), estimated to have occurred between 5 and 1.7 Ma, resulted in large genomic insertions on chromosome 5H, some spanning over 400 kb and containing TEs and protein-coding genes41. Here, we identified Panicoideae-derived nuclear genes across 20 diploid Hordeum species, with H. vulgare serving as a negative control39,41. Our analysis revealed 611 foreign genes that corresponded to 126 orthogroups, predominantly matching Paspalum (63%) and Panicum (22%) (Extended Data Fig. 7a and Supplementary Tables 14 and 15). The extent of HGT varied, with Hordeum flexuosum carrying the highest number of foreign genes (68 genes corresponding to 43 orthogroups) (Extended Data Fig. 7a). These findings align with studies indicating that grasses frequently exchange genetic material42,43. HGT frequency correlates with Hordeum phylogeny, with Mediterranean and West Asian species exhibiting fewer transferred genes than their South American counterparts. This supports the hypothesis that HGT has a cumulative impact on eukaryotic evolution44. The presence of a single panicoid gene in H. bulbosum and H. murinum can be explained by the introgression of chromosomal segment 1H from I genome species, rather than by an early HGT event predating the diversification of Hordeum (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 6c). Chromosomal mapping indicates that horizontally transferred genes are distributed across all seven Hordeum chromosomes, with chromosome 5H carrying the largest number (Extended Data Fig. 7b). These genes are significantly enriched in the distal regions of chromosome arms. Although distal regions generally contain higher local gene densities, negative binomial regression analysis demonstrated that gene density explains only a small fraction of the observed variation in HGT abundance (pseudo-R2 = 0.034; Supplementary Fig. 61), indicating that higher gene density alone cannot account for the distal enrichment of HGT genes. Although co-transfer of genes remains uncertain, previous research suggests that large fragments of foreign DNA may be transferred together41,43. A substantial fraction (82 out of 126) of Panicoideae-derived orthogroups lack native Hordeum homologues, indicating novel gene acquisition. Functional annotation suggests that these genes may have roles in key physiological processes such as auxin transport, light response and transcription regulation. RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) analysis detected at least one expressed HGT gene in 73 out of 126 orthogroups (Extended Data Fig. 7c and Supplementary Table 16). The potential adaptive significance of these genes warrants further investigation. Our genus-wide analysis establishes Hordeum as a model system for studying the evolutionary impact of HGT.

In a recent development, the genome assembly sizes of Hordeum species range from 2.90 Gb to 10.9 Gb and are highly correlated with previous flow-cytometric estimates45 (Fig. 3a). After accounting for the direct effects of polyploidization, the haplomes exhibit pseudomolecule sizes ranging from 2.85 Gb to 4.68 Gb. Apart from a 19 Mb duplication detected in the subgenome of H. jubatum, no large duplication events were identified (Supplementary Figs. 59–60). A strong correlation was observed between total TE content and haplome size (Fig. 3b), confirming that TE accumulation has significantly contributed to genome size variation in Hordeum. LTR retrotransposons were identified as the primary drivers of these changes, although DNA transposons also had a role (Fig. 3c). Correlation analyses of individual transposon superfamilies demonstrated that multiple TE families contributed to genome size variation, although overall TE abundance remained the strongest predictor of haplome size (Supplementary Fig. 62a). We selected transposons annotated in the TREP database with an average content above 20 Mb and examined their variation across different Hordeum haplomes. These TE families clearly differentiated the major evolutionary lineages of Hordeum (Supplementary Fig. 62b). To investigate lineage-specific TE dynamics in greater detail, we focused on three LTR retrotransposon families (BARE1, Sabrina and BAGY2) and used TEpop46 to reconstruct their diversification histories. TE subfamilies correspond closely to the major Hordeum clades (Fig. 3d and Extended Data Fig. 8a,b), demonstrating lineage-specific amplification histories that contributed to genome size evolution.

To investigate TE evolution following polyploidization, we compared the TE landscapes of three independently formed tetraploid genomes with those of their diploid progenitors. The three polyploid species exhibited distinct evolutionary trajectories. In H. murinum, TE expansion was minimal (Extended Data Fig. 8c and Supplementary Table 17). In H. jubatum, both subgenomes were smaller than their diploid progenitors (Fig. 3e and Supplementary Table 17). By contrast, Hordeum secalinum experienced extensive TE proliferation, resulting in substantial genome expansion (Extended Data Fig. 8d and Supplementary Table 17). Notably, LTR/Gypsy elements indicated the greatest expansion relative to the diploid progenitors and therefore contributed most to genome expansion in H. secalinum (Supplementary Table 17). Additionally, the Vagabond TE family showed renewed activity following tetraploidization, with significantly higher activity in the tetraploid genome than in either its diploid progenitors or the alternative subgenome (Extended Data Fig. 8e and Supplementary Figs. 63 and 64). To avoid bias introduced by large segmental exchanges between subgenomes, we excluded genomic regions inferred to originate from ancient hybridization before estimating TE insertion ages (Supplementary Table 13 and Supplementary Fig. 65). Although subgenome differentiation alone does not permit precise dating of tetraploid formation, post-polyploid TE dynamics can be reconstructed from TE insertions. Specifically, we inferred the timing of subgenome fusion from the insertion ages of full-length TEs shared exclusively between subgenomes but absent from their respective diploid progenitors (Fig. 3f, Extended Data Fig. 8f,g and Supplementary Figs. 65 and 66). These shared insertions must have occurred after polyploid formation, thereby providing temporal information on the origin of the polyploid genomes and subsequent TE activity. Our findings underscore that TE content is the primary determinant of genome size variation in Hordeum. Tetraploidization does not always lead to genome expansion relative to diploid ancestors; we also observed genome contraction. Nevertheless, post-polyploid LTR insertions provided an independent estimate of the timing of polyploid formation and newly introduced insights into the evolutionary history of tetraploid and hexaploid Hordeum genomes.

Industry observers note that whole-genome MSAs provide a framework for investigating sequence conservation and divergence across species. We therefore generated a whole-genome MSA of Hordeum haplomes using Progressive Cactus47. In total, we identified 170.4 Mb of shared aligned sequences across the Hordeum genomes (Extended Data Fig. 9a). As expected, rapidly evolving pericentromeric regions showed fewer alignments, whereas chromosome distal ends exhibited higher alignment densities (Extended Data Fig. 9b). The rapid contraction of these alignments is probably due to substantial reshaping of Hordeum genomes by TE activity over the past 12 million years. To further investigate sequence conservation across different functional genomic regions, we analysed open chromatin regions identified by assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with sequencing (ATAC–seq) together with annotated genomic features in eight Hordeum haplomes (Supplementary Table 18). Untranslated region sequences were the most highly conserved non-coding regions and were lost at a slower rate before the divergence of barley and wheat. By contrast, open chromatin regions exhibited a loss pattern similar to introns, whereas promoter regions underwent more rapid turnover (Extended Data Fig. 10a). Additionally, we used phastCons to identify 74.7 Mb of conserved elements across Hordeum genomes (Extended Data Fig. 10b,c). Among all conserved bases, 69.0% overlapped annotated genes and 6.0% overlapped open chromatin regions. Conversely, 44.7% of annotated gene bases and 31.9% of open chromatin bases overlapped conserved elements. Conserved elements were significantly enriched in both annotated genes (odds ratio = 138.0) and open chromatin regions (odds ratio = 27.4), with substantially stronger enrichment in genes, indicating stronger evolutionary constraint on coding sequences than on regulatory regions (Extended Data Fig. 10c).

Overall, our findings indicate that regulatory elements undergo substantially faster evolutionary turnover than coding sequences, generating extensive regulatory variation that may provide a valuable source of alleles for barley improvement. By contrast, the high conservation of coding genes provides opportunities for comparative functional analyses and cross-species transfer of biological knowledge.

In cultivated barley, spring and winter growth habits are largely determined by the vernalization genes VERNALIZATION 1 (VRN1), a MADS-box transcription factor, and VERNALIZATION 2 (VRN2), which is encoded by a cluster of zinc-finger/CCT (ZCCT) genes. In winter barley, prolonged cold induces VRN1 expression, which represses VRN2 and thereby permits flowering48,49. Flowering of winter varieties requires repression of VRN2 by cold-induced VRN1 (ref. 49). By contrast, spring barleys often carry deletions in the first intron of VRN1 and lack VRN2, eliminating their vernalization requirement50,51,52. Intermediate facultative types combine the vernalization-sensitive VRN1 with a non-functional VRN2 locus. It remains largely unexplored how wild Hordeum species regulate flowering across diverse climates.

Examining VRN1 in Hordeum genomes revealed extensive variation in the promoter and the regulatory first intron (5.7 kb to 19.5 kb) caused by TEs (Supplementary Table 19). To assess the functional effect of this variation, we recorded flowering time of 14 wild Hordeum species and 4 barley controls under non-vernalizing conditions with a 14 h light:10 h dark photoperiod (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 11a). Notably, Hordeum cordobense and Hordeum muticum flowered rapidly (approximately 61 days), surpassing spring barley cultivars (Fig. 4a). Both species share a unique 79-bp deletion in VRN1 intron 1 critical region51, suggesting a role in reducing the vernalization requirement (Extended Data Fig. 11b). All species contained the VRN2 locus with one to seven ZCCT copies (Supplementary Table 19). A key finding was an inverted repeat of two ZCCT genes in H. cordobense, Hordeum californicum, H. muticum and H. jubatum (Supplementary Fig. 67). Because inverted repeats may trigger RNA interference (RNAi)53, we expected silencing of VRN2 and a spring-type phenotype. Surprisingly, only H. cordobense and H. muticum flowered early (Fig. 4a,c and Extended Data Fig. 11a). Detailed analysis of H. cordobense revealed a non-functional ZCCT-1 owing to a premature stop codon, and the absence of a polyadenylation signal in the ZCCT-2/ZCCT-3 inverted repeat linker, enabling read-through transcription (detected as an aberrant mRNA transcript), hairpin RNA formation and small RNA production (Fig. 4b,d, Extended Data Fig. 11c and Supplementary Fig. 68). Winter-type H. californicum carried additional functional ZCCT copies and a polyadenylation signal in the inverted repeat linker that probably prevented RNAi, thus maintaining the VRN2 repressive function (Fig. 4b,e). This aligns with the expression of VRN1, VRN2 and their target FLOWERING LOCUS T1 (FT1) in the analysed species (Fig. 4f). These findings highlight that genetic diversity shapes vernalization in Hordeum. The studied spring-like accessions carry the 79-bp VRN1 deletion alongside disrupted or silenced VRN2, whereas winter-like genotypes retain functional ZCCT copies. Together, our results indicate that adaptation to spring growth habit in wild Hordeum species has targeted the same genes and variant types as in cultivated barley, pointing to conserved mechanisms of flowering-time adaptation.
