DAG, days after germination. b, Structure of the VRN2 locus in H. cordobense with three ZCCT genes, and in H. californicum with six ZCCT genes. The scheme is not to scale. Teal rectangles represent exons, asterisks indicate stop codons, purple ovals are TEs, the black dots indicate a polyadenylation (p(A)) signal and sand-coloured regions are inverted repeats. c, Phenotypes of four Hordeum species with contrasting VRN2 locus structures at 65 and 200 DAG. Arrows mark visible spikes. d,e, Mean distribution of RNA-seq and small RNA (sRNA)-sequencing reads over three biological replicates normalized to bins per million (BPM) mapped reads in H. cordobense (d) and H. californicum (e) across the VRN2 locus at 14 and 28 DAG. Read mapping at the H. cordobense ZCCT-3 locus suggests the presence of improperly spliced, probably aberrant transcripts. f, Transcripts per million (TPM) values at 14 and 28 DAG in H. cordobense and H. californicum.

In a recent development, the glume is a distinctive floral organ in the grass family, which lacks a direct counterpart in dicotyledonous plants54. It appears as one or multiple pairs of bract-like structures subtending single or multiple fertile florets. Glume size and shape vary widely, from large lemma-like structures in Triticum species to rudimentary axillary buds in Oryza. In wild grasses, glume morphology influences seed dispersal, reproductive success and defence against biotic stress55. In cultivated cereals, domestication has favoured reduced glume size and roughness, facilitating easier threshing. In Hordeum, each floret possesses a pair of glumes positioned on the periaxial side, with considerable variation in length, width and awn extension across species (Fig. 5a). Transcriptomic profiling of five diploid species carrying the I genome (H. erectifolium, Hordeum pusillum, Hordeum intercedens H. stenostachys and Hordeum euclaston) identified spike-specific genes expressed in young spikes at early (Waddington stages 3–6 (W3–6)) and late (W9–10) developmental stages56 (Supplementary Table 21). Genes were classified as spike-specific if their transcript abundance in the remaining 11 out of 13 analysed tissues was less than 5% of their combined expression in the 2 spike samples. Five genes were consistently expressed across species, suggesting conserved regulatory mechanisms (Extended Data Fig. 12a and Supplementary Table 21). These genes encode a C2H2-type zinc-finger transcription factor, an auxin response factor, a TCP transcription factor, a subtilisin protease (SBT) and a MADS-box transcription factor. Three were predominantly expressed during early spike development, one at later stages and one at both stages (Extended Data Fig. 12b). In rice, loss-of-function mutations in NONSTOP GLUMES1 (NSG1), the orthologue of the C2H2-type zinc-finger transcription factor, result in uncontrolled glume growth57. Amino acid variations in this gene across Hordeum species along with glume variations suggested a relevance in regulating glume development (Fig. 5a and Supplementary Fig. 69). Mutations in its cultivated barley orthologue (EOG1) lead to the elongated outer glume (eog1) phenotype (Fig. 5b). These mutants develop enlarged glumes on the central fertile spikelet, with glume awns extending to lemma-awn length, giving the spike a brushy appearance (Extended Data Fig. 12c,d). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) revealed developmental divergence between wild-type and eog1 mutants as early as W3.5 (Fig. 5c). By integrating comparative genomics across Hordeum with tissue-specific expression data and cultivated barley mutant resources, we identify EOG1 as a conserved regulator of glume development.

It has been revealed that a, Central spikelet from representative Hordeum species exhibiting glume morphology diversity. gl, glume. Scale bars, 500 μm. b, Allelic variations of a C2H2-type zinc-finger transcription factor gene (HORVU.MOREX.r3.2HG0170820.1) in cultivated barley (H. vulgare) lead to glume elongation. The rectangle denotes the exon or full-length coding sequence, with the red rectangle indicating the C2H2-type zinc-finger domain. The asterisk marks a premature stop codon. HTX (Hatiexie) represents the wild type, which exhibits suppressed glume development, whereas the mutants exhibit elongation in glume growth. The mutant allele lep-e.1 (ref. 59) carries a deletion allele of the EOG1 gene. Scale bars, 1 cm. c, Differentiation on the spikelet morphogenesis along Waddington stage between the wild-type HTX and the induced mutant M9630. W3, glume primordial present; W3.5, floret primordial present; W5, carpel extending. le, lemma. Scale bars, 100 μm.

Sources indicate that the chromosome-scale genome assemblies presented here provide a foundation for investigating the evolutionary history of the genus Hordeum. Chromosome-scale resolution enables us to investigate how structural variations have shaped genome evolution, particularly in disrupting chromosomal collinearity. Traditionally, grass genomes were thought to possess relatively stable chromosome structures58; however, our findings challenge this assumption. Extensive structural variations and chromosomal rearrangements have contributed substantially to genomic divergence, ultimately resulting in the near-complete loss of collinearity in proximal regions. These rearrangements not only mark evolutionary divergence but also provide insights into the processes underlying speciation within Hordeum. Structural variations accumulated at markedly different rates across chromosome regions. Whereas proximal regions exhibit high variability, distal regions evolve more slowly. This uneven evolutionary rate has preserved footprints of ancient hybridization events across the genus, offering a historical record of interspecific gene flow. These findings provide empirical evidence for ancient hybridization and genome fusion during Hordeum evolution and establish a framework for identifying compatible genomic segments in future interspecific breeding efforts.

Recent findings suggest that nevertheless, whether the large inversions identified in this study contribute to adaptive evolution, reproductive isolation or other phenotypic consequences remains unknown and warrants future functional investigation. Whole-genome MSAs enabled us to compare genome-wide conservation across Hordeum species. Compared with animal genomes, which often display strong interspecies conservation, plant genomes—especially within rapidly evolving genera such as Hordeum—undergo dynamic changes driven by short generation times and rapid transposon expansion. These processes fuel the ongoing remodelling of plant genomes, resulting in high variability even among closely related taxa. Despite this rapid evolution, many genes remain conserved, whereas regulatory elements exhibit considerable turnover. This contrast offers unique opportunities: lineage-specific regulatory innovation can be harnessed for crop improvement, while core gene functions are retained. For example, regulatory elements associated with vernalization responses were found to vary across Hordeum species, suggesting that novel regulatory variants could be introduced into cultivated barley to fine-tune flowering behaviour. Beyond expanding genomic resources for Hordeum, this work provides a framework for investigating structural genome evolution, reconstructing complex evolutionary histories and harnessing genetic and regulatory diversity for barley improvement.

Recent findings suggest that plant material was obtained from genebanks at Institut für Pflanzgenetik und Kulturpflanzenforschung (IPK) Gatersleben, the US Department of Agriculture and the Nordic Genetic Resource Center. Accession numbers are listed in Supplementary Table 1.

It has been revealed that plants were grown under greenhouse conditions and high molecular weight (HMW) DNA was isolated from young leaf tissue according to published protocols10,60. Construction of HiFi libraries and Circular Consensus Sequencing using the PacBio Sequel IIe instrument (Pacific Biosciences) were essentially as described previously19. HiFi sequencing was done at IPK Gatersleben, Genomics and Transcriptomics Laboratory, Heinrich Heine University, Berry Genomics Co., Novogene and the University of Wisconsin Biotechnology Center DNA Sequencing Facility.

According to recent reports, in situ Hi-C libraries were prepared from young seedlings according to the previously published protocol, using DpnII for the digestion of crosslinked chromatin. Libraries were prepared as described61. Samples were quantified62 and sequenced with standard protocols from Illumina using Illumina NovaSeq 6000 devices (Illumina) at IPK Gatersleben and Novogene.

Industry observers note that A clone of the same H. erectifolium individual plant that was sequenced using PacBio HiFi was used for the construction of the optical genome map (OGM). A total of 2.5 million nuclei, purified from young leaves by flow cytometry, were embedded in agarose miniplugs and treated with proteinase K, following the protocol of Šimková et al.63. A total of 525 ng of HMW DNA was directly labelled at DLE-1 recognition sites using the standard Bionano Prep Direct Label and Stain protocol (Bionano) and analysed on the Bionano Saphyr platform. The resulting dataset, comprising 1.5 Tb of single-molecule data with an N50 of 247 kb, provided approximately 341× coverage of the H. erectifolium genome. This dataset was used to generate a de novo OGM assembly using Bionano Solve software (v3.6.1_11162020) with the standard configuration file optArguments_nonhaplotype_noES_noCut_DLE1_saphyr.xml.

To improve the contiguity of the PacBio HiFi assembly, the automatic hybrid scaffold pipeline integrated in Bionano Solve was run using the OGM assembly. The default DLE-1 Hybrid Scaffold configuration file was applied with the ‘resolve conflict’ option for conflict resolution. Conflicts between the sequence assembly and the OGM were manually curated and the pipeline was subsequently re-run using a modified conflict_cut_status.txt file.

Plants were grown under greenhouse conditions and total RNA was isolated from different tissues and developmental stages (Supplementary Table 5) using the RNAeasy Plant Mini Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) or with Trizol reagent (Invitrogen) according to the manufacturers’ protocols. RNA-seq was performed on replicated bulk sample representing a specific developmental stage or tissue type. RNA-seq of individual samples and PacBio IsoSeq of RNA pools was performed as described previously10. Library construction and sequencing on Illumina NovaSeq 6000 devices (Illumina RNA-seq) and PacBio Sequel IIe (instruments) was done at IPK Gatersleben, Biomarker Technologies (BMK), the Genomics and Transcriptomics Laboratory at Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf, Kazusa DNA Research Institute or Berry Genomics. The PacBio IsoSeq sequencing data was processed with the isoseq3 (v3.8.2) pipeline (PacBio - IsoSeq3, 2018/2024). The ploy-A tails were trimmed and concatenated transcripts removed with refine -require-polya-min-polya-length 12 teloprime.fasta. To generate non-redundant transcripts, we mapped the full-length non-concatenated reads were mapped to the genome with pbmm2 (v1.10.0) align -preset ISOSEQ -sort -bam-index CSI and redundant transcripts collapsed with isoseq3 collapse -do-not-collapse-extra-5exons.

According to recent reports, pacBio HiFi reads were assembled using hifiasm (v0.13-r308 or v0.15.5-r350 or v0.16.1-r375)64. Pseudomolecules were constructed with the TRITEX pipeline26,27, and chimeric contigs or orientation errors were corrected based on manual inspection of Hi-C contact matrices. For allotetraploid species, subgenomes were phased using a previously developed haplotype-resolved genome assembly strategy10. The origin of the subgenomes and their potential ancestral contributors were previously investigated in detail by Brassac et al.1 To classify subgenomes in the polyploid genome, Mash (v2.3)65 was used to calculate pairwise chromosomal similarities between polyploid chromosomes and candidate ancestral genomes. The resulting distance matrix was used to infer subgenome origin and relationships. In species with high heterozygosity or outcrossing (H. brevisubulatum and H. murinum BBC2017), Hi-C data were incorporated during hifiasm (v0.15.5-r350)64 assembly to collapse haplotypes and assemble a representative haploid genome. Except for H. erectifolium, whose primary contigs were first hybrid-scaffolded using a Bionano optical map, followed by pseudomolecule construction with Hi-C data and the TRITEX pipeline30. Chloroplast genomes were assembled following previously published protocols10. HiFi reads were aligned to the barley cv. Morex chloroplast genome (GenBank accession EF115541) using minimap2 (v2.24-r1122)66 with the parameters -ax map-hifi–secondary=no–sam-hit-only. Alignments with mapping quality <30 were discarded. Aligned reads were converted to FASTQ format using SAMtools (v1.16.1)67 and assembled with Canu (v2.1.1)68 in PacBio HiFi mode with genome sizes from 120 to 400 kb in 10-kb increments. Circular sequences were identified and trimmed using BEDTools (v2.30.0)69 and annotated with GeSeq70. Fully annotated assemblies were aligned to the Morex chloroplast genome using MUMmer4 (v4.0.0beta2)71, and start positions and orientations of the SSC region were adjusted to match the reference using seqkit (v0.9.1)72. k-mer frequencies were calculated using Jellyfish(v2.2.6)73 and analysed with findGSE(v1.94)74 to estimate genome characteristics. Assembly quality, including QV and k-mer completeness, was evaluated using Merqury(v1.3)75.

Industry observers note that we performed de novo structural gene prediction, confidence classification and functional annotation, following the protocol described in Mascher et al.28. As evidences we used RNA-seq and IsoSeq data as described under above and Poales-filtered protein sequences downloaded from UniProt76 (July 2023). An additional consolidation step was carried out using the liftoff77 tool. In brief, all predicted gene models from one species were lifted over to all other genomes. Using Mikado78, we selected the best mapped gene models and unified all gene predictions accordingly. We classified predicted proteins into high and low-confidence categories. High-confidence proteins had over 80% coverage and were complete, either with significant hits in UniMag or UniPoa but not PTREP (https://trep-db.uzh.ch). Low-confidence proteins were incomplete with hits in UniMag or UniPoa but not PTREP, or were complete without hits in any database.

We benchmarked the annotations with BUSCO (v5.8.0)79 (dataset: poales_odb12), OMARK (omamer verision 2.1.0/omark v0.3.1)80 and psauron (v1.0.6)81.

Sources indicate that orthogroups based on the primary protein sequences from 27 annotated Hordeum accessions were calculated using Orthofinder (v2.5.5)82. The scripts for the calculation of core, shell and cloud genes are deposited in the repository at https://github.com/PGSB-HMGU/BPGv2. Core genes contain at least 1 gene model from all 27 compared accessions. Shell genes contain gene models from at least 2 Hordeum accessions and at most 26. Genes clustered with genes only from the same genotype were defined as cloud genes. Annotations of H. vulgare Morex and H. bulbosum were not included during the consolidation step. Therefore, to counteract any potential over- or under-presentation of these two species in any of the core, shell or cloud categories, we aligned all cloud genes for H. vulgare cv. Morex and H. bulbosum back to all other genomes and corrected for any missing genes. Gene Ontology-term enrichments were conducted with goatools (v1.4.4)83. Gene-based collinearity plots were drawn with GENESPACE84.

According to recent reports, the RGAugury (v2.2)85 pipeline was used to identify from our annotation and classify nucleotide-binding site (NB-ARC) domain-encoding genes into different subgroups, based on domain and motif structures: TNL contain TIR, NBS and LRR domains; CNL contain CC, NBS and LRR domains; RNL contain RPW8, NBS and LRR domains; RN contain RPW8 and NBS domains only; NL contain NBS and LRR domains but lack TIR, CC and RPW8; TN contain TIR and NBS domains only; CN contain CC and NBS domains only; and NBS-only genes contain only the NBS domain. TIR, NBS, LRR, CC and RPW8 refer to the Toll/Interleukin-1 Receptor-like, Nucleotide-Binding Site, Leucine-Rich Repeat, Coiled-Coil and Resistance to Powdery Mildew 8-like domains, respectively. An NLR gene cluster is defined based on the genomic proximity of NLR genes. Specifically, any two NLR genes located within 500 kb of each other are grouped into the same cluster by bedtools (v2.30.0)69. NLR genes were then grouped into clusters using bedtools (v2.30.0)69 merge with a maximum intergenic distance of 250 kb. Only clusters comprising no fewer than three NLR genes were retained. Pan-NLR analysis was performed based on orthogroups identified using OrthoFinder (v2.5.5)82 across all NLR genes. Core orthogroups are defined as orthogroups that contain at least one gene model from each of the compared Hordeum accessions. Shell orthogroups include gene models from at least two and at most 26Hordeum accessions. Gene models that were not assigned to any orthogroup (singletons) or were grouped only with genes from the same genotype were classified as cloud genes.

Open reading frames longer than 100 codons were searched for the presence of PPR and mTERF motifs using hmmsearch from the HMMER suite (http://hmmer.org) using hidden Markov models as defined in Cheng et al.86. for the PPR family and PF02536 from the Pfam 32.0 database (http://pfam.xfam.org)87 for the mTERF motif. Downstream processing of the hmmsearch results for the PPR proteins followed the pipeline described in Gutmann et al.88. The RfCTD domain recently identified as a unique feature of RFL-PPRs89 was included in the gene annotations. P-class and PLS-class genes with scores below 100 and 240, respectively, were excluded from the annotation as they are unlikely to represent functional PPR genes, as defined previously (IWGSC 2018)90.

The analyses described here used a number of tools from the toolkits vg (v1.61.0)91, odgi (v0.8.3-26-gbc7742ed)92, bcftools (v1.21)67 and seqkit (v2.9.0)72. All scripts used for graph construction and analysis are available at https://github.com/cropgeeks/panHordeum. Owing to computational limitations, we built an alignment of Hordeum whole genomes with Cactus47. We selected H. marinum BCC 2001 over H. marinum H559 on the basis of its higher assembly quality. Genome haplomes were soft-masked with bedtools69 using their respective repeat annotations. The guide tree required for the Cactus alignment was taken from the Orthofinder93 output generated as part of this study. Apart from setting appropriate resource parameters (that is, threads, memory and disk), we ran Cactus with default parameters. We transformed the resulting whole-genome alignment into a super-pangenome graph using hal2vg (https://github.com/ComparativeGenomicsToolkit/hal2vg), with the –noAncestors flag, and then further processed it with vg convert to get the final pangenome graph in GFA format (https://github.com/GFA-spec/GFA-spec). We computed basic graph statistics using odgi stats with the –summarize option, which included graph size, number of nodes, edges, paths and steps. To characterize the conservation of the different segments of the graph, we classified nodes as core, shell, or cloud. A node was considered ‘core’ if it was traversed by all samples’ paths, ‘cloud’ if it was traversed by a single sample’s path, and ‘shell’ otherwise. The same classification was done at the base level. Both computations were performed using the odgi toolkit (implementation details in class_stats.sh). To evaluate the agreement of haplotype sequences with their representation in the graph, we first extracted the linear sequences of all haplotypes as encoded in the graph using odgi paths with the –fasta option. These sequences were subsequently partitioned by source genome using seqkit grep, creating direct pairwise comparisons between input genomes and their graph-encoded counterparts. For each genome pair, we performed exact sequence matching, confirming whether each input sequence (or its reverse complement) was precisely preserved in the graph-encoded version (implementation details available in script fidelity.py). We computed pangenome graph growth curves based on the full graph using odgi heaps with 100 permutations of the input genomes. Results were plotted using script heaps_fit.R distributed with the odgi toolkit92. Whole-graph analysis turned out to be computationally prohibitive (job runtime limits and/or memory requirements) for several of the required tools from the vg and odgi toolkits, given a graph of this size and complexity. We therefore extracted subgraphs equating to individual chromosome paths for H. vulgare cv. Morex, which we used as the basis for all variant analyses. We used vg chunk for subgraph extraction. Variants were called from the chromosome-level subgraphs directly, using vg deconstruct. This generated VCF output containing the full range of variant sizes. To prepare structural variants from the graph for further analysis we broadly followed the variant decomposition approach used by the Human Pangenome Consortium94. This involved the removal of top-level variants of length >100,000 bp with vcfbub (https://github.com/pangenome/vcfbub), realigning alternate alleles against the reference for each variant using vcfwave (vcflib v1.0.2)95, and finally normalizing the resulting variants with bcftools norm67. We then added variant length information (SVLEN) to the VCF files with a custom script to allow extraction of structural variants based on the length difference between reference and alternate allele (>50 bp) and classified structural variations as deletions or insertions based on the directionality of the difference (insertion: string length REF  string length ALT). The resulting VCF files were converted to BED format with bcftools query. Variant density plots were computed with custom R scripts using ggplot2 (v3.5.1)96. To explore the possibility of using the graph for read mapping and genotyping, we attempted to index the graph using vg gbwt/vg index/vg minimizer. This turned out to be computationally prohibitive in terms of job runtime limits on two separate compute facilities used, and thus we were unable to use the graph for the valuation of read mapping. We conducted graph-based conservation analysis with Pansel97, a tool used for calculation of diversity/conservation metrics directly from pan-genome graphs. The default bin size of 1kbp was used, along with all other parameters on default settings. Results were plotted using ggplot2 (v3.5.1)96.

Sources indicate that single-copy genes were identified using BUSCO (v5.4.6)79 in B. distachyon (v3.0)98, O. sativa (IRGSP-1.0)99, S. bicolor (NCBIv3)99, T. monococcum100, H. vulgare FT11 (ref. 19) and the 29 Hordeum haplomes collected in this study. Protein sequences of BUSCO single-copy genes present in all 34 haplomes were concatenated and aligned using MAFFT (v7.490)101. Well-aligned regions were filtered using Gblocks (v0.91b)102 with parameters -t=extractedp -b4 = 5 -b5=h. A maximum-likelihood phylogenetic tree was then constructed using RAxML (v8.2.12)103 with the PROTGAMMAWAG substitution model and the rapid bootstrap algorithm with 100 replicates. To facilitate genome-wide alignment, all 34 haplomes were masked using RepeatMasker (v4.1.1; http://www.repeatmasker.org) with a pan-genome TE library generated by panEDTA. The masked genomes and the inferred species tree were then used as input for Cactus (v2.6.5)47 to generate whole-genome MSAs. The loss rate of genomic elements was defined as the size of the reconstructed ancestral sequence at the corresponding genomic position in the multiple genome alignment.

It has been revealed that to precisely construct phylogenetic trees and estimate divergence times within the genus Hordeum, we included four additional outgroup genomes: B. distachyon (v3.0)98, O. sativa (IRGSP-1.0)99, S. bicolor (NCBIv3)104 (all downloaded from Ensembl Plants; https://plants.ensembl.org/index.html) and T. monococcum100 (https://wheat.pw.usda.gov/GG3/pangenome). We constructed phylogenetic trees using four approaches. The first two methods were based on whole-genome single-copy genes. Orthologous genes were identified from the genomes of our 34 Hordeum haplomes and four outgroup genomes using OrthoFinder (v2.5.5)82, yielding 2,198 single-copy genes. For the concatenation-based approach, the CDS sequences of these genes were concatenated and aligned with MAFFT (v7.490)101, and well-aligned regions were retained using Gblocks (v0.91b)102 with the parameters -t=extractedp, -b4 = 5, -b5=h; phylogenetic inference was then performed in IQ-TREE (v2.2.2.6)105. For the coalescence-based approach, the CDS sequences of each single-copy gene were aligned separately using MAFFT (v7.490)101, high-quality regions were selected with Gblocks (v0.91b)102 using the same parameters, individual gene trees were reconstructed with IQ-TREE (v2.2.2.6)105, and a species tree was inferred from these gene trees using ASTRAL-Pro3 (CASTLES-Pro, v1.23.3.6)106. The remaining two methods were based on whole-genome MSAs generated with Cactus. In the CASTER-pair (CASTLES-Pro, v1.23.3.6)107 approach, the whole-genome MSA was used to infer a phylogenetic tree rooted with S. bicolor, while in the CASTER-site (CASTLES-Pro, v1.23.3.6)107 approach, the whole-genome MSA was analysed similarly but using site-based inference, also rooted with S. bicolor.

It has been revealed that to estimate divergence times, genomic regions showing strong phylogenetic discordance (nRF > 0.21) were first excluded based on the genome-wide discordance analysis. 4DTV sites were extracted from MSAs of single-copy genes. Divergence times between barley and outgroup species were obtained from the TimeTree database (https://timetree.org/)108. Finally, species divergence times within the genus Hordeum were estimated using the MCMCtree program in PAML (v4.4)109.

Sources indicate that we excluded multiple haplomes from the same species and retained a final set of 32 Hordeum haplomes for comparative analysis. All haplomes pairs were aligned against each other using minimap2 (v2.24-r1122)66 with the parameters -2 -K 5 G -f 0.005 -x asm10, and the resulting alignments were stored in PAF format for visualization via dot plots. For each reference haplomes, we calculated the alignment coverage in non-overlapping 5 Mb windows, considering only alignments with a mapping quality greater than 20. Coverage values were normalized across the haplomes by the average coverage to produce normalized coverage profiles. In species that diverged more than 9 Ma, a bimodal distribution of normalized coverage was observed, allowing a threshold of 0.5 to distinguish distal and proximal regions (Extended Data Fig. 3b,c). Finally, genome-wide alignment and normalized coverage profiles were used to manually define the size and boundaries of proximal and distal regions across all species. Reverse-orientation alignments were extracted as indicators of putative inversion events. Two metrics were calculated for each pairwise comparison: (1) the number of reverse-orientation alignments per Mb and (2) the proportion of bases covered by reverse-orientation alignments. These metrics were separately calculated for proximal and distal chromosomal regions to compare the rates of inversion accumulation during species divergence. Linear regression models including divergence time, chromosomal region type (proximal or distal) and their interaction term were used to evaluate differences in the accumulation rates of reverse-orientation alignments between regions.

All other Hordeum genomes were aligned to the MorexV3 (ref. 28) reference genome using wfmash (v0.9.1-3; https://github.com/waveygang/wfmash) with the parameters -p 90 -l 0. Inversions were then identified using SyRI (v1.5.5)110 with parameters -F P -f–nosnp. Only inversions larger than 2 Mb and located outside of the proximal regions were retained for further analysis.

Industry observers note that based on the 2,198 single-copy orthologues identified in the section ‘Phylogeny and divergence time estimation’ and using the genome-wide concatenated single-copy gene tree as a reference, we conducted sliding-window gene tree analyses (Extended Data Fig. 6a). All single-copy genes were grouped into non-overlapping windows of 25 genes with a step size of 2 genes. Within each window, protein sequences were aligned using MAFFT (v7.490)101, and well-aligned regions were retained using Gblocks (v0.91b)102 with the parameters -t=extractedp -b4 = 5 -b5=h. Local window trees were built with FastTree (v2.1.11)111 (default GTR + CAT, 20 rate categories), starting from neighbour-joining trees and optimized with minimum-evolution and nearest-neighbour interchange moves; branch support was calculated using Shimodaira–Hasegawa-like values. Each resulting tree was rooted with S. bicolor as the outgroup using ETE3 (v3.1.2)112, and the nRF distance was calculated against the reference tree using the parameter –min_support_src 90. The nRF metric quantifies topological dissimilarity between trees, with values ranging from 0 (identical topology) to 1 (completely different topologies). Based on the nRF distribution, we identified 0.21 as a threshold to separate background from discordant signal peaks (Extended Data Fig. 6b). To evaluate the robustness of discordant region detection, we repeated the sliding-window analyses using alternative parameter settings (30 genes with step sizes of 1 and 5 genes). The major discordance peaks were consistently recovered across different window sizes and step lengths, indicating that peak detection was not sensitive to parameter selection (Supplementary Fig. 52). Genomic regions containing at least 10 overlap windows with nRF ≥ 0.21 were defined as candidate introgressed regions. For each candidate region, we reconstructed local phylogenetic trees using the same procedure as for the genome-wide tree. The topological comparison of these local trees with the reference tree enabled the inference of introgression origins. The AU test113 implemented in IQ-TREE (v2.2.2.6)105, was used to compare local reference trees and local phylogenetic trees. A P value (p-AU) lower than 0.05 indicated that the tree was significantly rejected.

Genomes of 20 diploid Hordeum species were searched for potential HGT genes from grasses of the subfamily Panicoideae. Regions of interest were identified in the genomes using BLAST (v2.12.0+)114 against four potential donor species: Panicum hallii (v3.2), Setaria italica (v2.2), Paspalum vaginatum (v3.1) and Paspalum notatum (GCA_036689595.1) (Supplementary Table 10). BLAST results were filtered to retain hits with a sequence identity of ≥95% and an alignment length of ≥150 bp. The same process was applied to H. vulgare cv. Morex (v3), which served as a negative control. H. vulgare is widely recognized as a species that lacks HGT genes from the Panicoideae subfamily39,41,42. Hits from potential donors that were found in both the Hordeum recipient genomes and H. vulgare were excluded from further analysis. This filtering was conducted using the intersect tool from BEDTools (v2.26.0)69, with an overlap threshold of 20%. Finally, the identified regions were compared with newly available annotations, and corresponding candidate genes were extracted. In this step, we identified 5,169 candidate genes.

Sources indicate that to verify the foreign (that is, Panicoideae) origin of the candidate HGT genes identified as described above, phylogenetic trees were constructed for each candidate. Homologues were retrieved from a set of representative Poaceae species and two outgroups (Ananas comosus and Musa acuminata) (Supplementary Table 10) using BLASTn (e-value cutoff of 10−10). The retrieved sequences were aligned with the Hordeum HGT gene candidates using MUSCLE (v3.8)115. The alignments were trimmed using trimAl (v1.2) with an automated trimming method116. Phylogenetic trees were constructed using PhyML (v3.1)117, with 1,000 bootstrap iterations and the GTR substitution model. The resulting trees were reviewed semi-automatically with the assistance of the Newick Utilities suite118. A candidate gene was considered a true HGT gene if the gene sequence was nested within the PACMAD clade. TE-related genes were filtered out and only high-confidence, protein-coding genes were retained for further analysis. Out of 5,169 candidate genes, 4,393 did not pass through the primary phylogenetic validation and 776 genes remained. Candidate genes that passed the first step of verification were cross-referenced with orthogroups previously created during pan-genome construction. For groups containing more than one candidate gene, a consensus sequence was generated using MAFFT (v7.520)102 for MSA, followed by the cons tool from EMBOSS (v6.5.7.0)119 to produce the consensus. These consensus sequences were subsequently used for BLASTn searches. Hits from at least five species, including minimally one from Panicoideae, were required for tree construction. Phylogenetic trees were then constructed as described above, using MAFFT as the aligner. Alignments and trees were reviewed manually: orthogroups supporting the HGT scenario were retained, and genes in these groups were classified as either foreign or native, based on their position on the tree. The neighbour of transferred genes was marked as presumed donor if the branch represented one genus or species, otherwise the donor was marked as unknown. The entire orthogroup was considered to have a native copy if it contained at least one gene marked ‘native’, regardless of which species that gene was present in.

Industry observers note that to determine the transfer times of genes during the evolutionary history of the lineage, an ancestral state reconstruction was conducted for each gene independently. The marginal ancestral state was inferred using the equal rate model120, applying the maximum-likelihood approach described by Pagel121 and implemented in the phytools package122. To ensure accuracy, the results were verified and adjusted for cases where genes were found in multiple tips but not in their common ancestor. In such instances, the presence of the gene was manually introduced at the ancestor node. For each node in the phylogenetic tree, both the originally reconstructed values and the manually adjusted values were visualized.

Genes from all orthogroups were annotated using eggNOG-mapper web server (v2.1.12)123,124. Gene Ontology terms were extracted for each group and enrichment analysis was performed using the clusterProfiler package (v4.14.3), with a significance threshold of an adjusted P value of 0.05 (ref. 125).

RNA-seq data for inflorescence, leaf and root tissues previously generated for 19 Hordeum species were used in this study (RNA-seq data for H. bulbosum were not available). Read trimming on quality (Q30) and removal of sequencing adapters were done using Trimmomatic (v0.32)126. Cleaned reads from each library were then mapped to the corresponding reference genome using the STAR aligner (v2.7.7a)127. Quantification of mapped reads was done using the subread package v1.5.2 with featureCounts (v2.0.1)128 followed by normalization using the trimmed mean of M-values (TMM) method implemented in the edgeR package (v4.2.1)129. Genes were considered to be expressed if TMM ≥ 1 in at least one tissue.

According to recent reports, structurally intact and fragmented TEs were annotated for each genome using the panEDTA (v0.1) pipeline31. In addition to the curated TREP database (https://trep-db.uzh.ch/)130, TE classification followed the EDTA ontology (https://github.com/oushujun/EDTA/blob/master/bin/TE_Sequence_Ontology.txt), with manual curation of TE categories. High-confidence gene models from H. vulgare cv. MorexV3 was supplied via the -cds parameter to exclude genic sequences from TE annotation. For each genome, the length, classification, insertion time and divergence metrics of intact LTR retrotransposons were extracted from the intact.gff3 and pass.list output files. To investigate TE family expansion and intergenomic relationships, we used the TEpop framework (https://github.com/wicker314/TEpop) to treat each TE as an individual sample for population structure analysis46. PCA was then performed using FlashPCA2 (ref. 131) to explore the major patterns of TE variation across Hordeum species. To infer the formation time of tetraploid genomes from TE bursts, full-length LTR/Copia elements were extracted from tetraploid assemblies and clustered using CD-HIT (v4.8.1)132 with the parameters -n 5 -c 0.9 -d 0 -aL 0.9 -aS 0.9 -g 1 based on sequence similarity. To avoid potential bias caused by large-scale segmental exchanges between subgenomes, genomic regions identified as exchanged segments were excluded from this analysis (Supplementary Table 13). TEs that were shared between polyploid subgenomes but absent from their corresponding diploid progenitors were defined as post-allopolyploidization insertions. The insertion time distributions of these elements were used to reconstruct TE dynamics after subgenome fusion, and the onset of the insertion peak was used to estimate the timing of polyploid genome formation.

To identify conserved elements across Hordeum genomes, outgroup species were removed from the HAL alignment file using halRemoveGenome in Cactus (v2.6.5). Genome-wide MSAs were then extracted in MAF format using cactus-hal2maf with the parameters “–chunkSize 1000000–noAncestors–onlyOrthologs–noDupes”, using MorexV3 as the reference genome. Alignment blocks containing fewer than 10 sequences were filtered out in MSAs. A neutral model of evolution was fitted to the Hordeum phylogeny using fourfold degenerate sites from chromosome 3H of barley, using phyloFit from the PHAST package (v1.4)133. Based on the genome-wide multiple alignments and the trained neutral model, conserved elements were identified using PhastCons with the “–most-conserved” flag. The conserved and non-conserved models were trained with a target genome coverage of 0.45, and the expected length of conserved elements was set to 8 bp.

ATAC–seq libraries were prepared from fresh leaf tissue at 3–5 leaf stage. Nuclei were isolated by fine chopping the tissue in isolation buffer (0.25 M sucrose, 10 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 10 mM MgCl2, 1% Trion X-100, 5 mM β-Mercaptoethanol) supplemented with 1× Halt Protease Inhibitor Cocktail (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Following isolation, nuclei were quantified via flow cytometry and 75,000 nuclei were subjected to tagmentation using the Tagment DNA Enzyme (TDE1, Illumina) at 37 °C for 30 min. Transposed DNA was purified using the MinElute PCR Purification Kit (Qiagen), libraries were amplified with NEBNext High-Fidelity 2x PCR Master Mix (Fresh England Biolabs), and the final library purification was performed using VAHTSTM DNA Clean Beads (Vazyme) according to standard protocols from the manufacturers. Libraries were quantified as described previously62 and sequenced (paired-end, 2× 151 cycles, Illumina NovaSeq 6000, IPK Gatersleben) following protocols provided by the manufacturer (Illumina).

Adapter trimming and quality filtering were performed using Trim Galore (v0.6.4_dev; https://github.com/FelixKrueger/TrimGalore.git) with the following parameters: -q 25–phred33–stringency 3–length 60–paired -j 10. Only read pairs with both ends retained were used in subsequent analyses. Trimmed reads were aligned to the reference genome using BWA (v0.7.17)134. The resulting SAM files were converted to BAM format and sorted using SAMtools (v1.10)67. Only properly paired reads with mapping quality ≥ 30 were retained (-f 2 -F 1804 -q 30), and further sorted by read name to enable mate information correction using samtools fixmate. Duplicate reads were marked using Picard MarkDuplicates (v2.21.9, https://broadinstitute.github.io/picard/) with VALIDATION_STRINGENCY=LENIENT and REMOVE_DUPLICATES=false. After marking, only properly paired, non-duplicate reads were retained and re-sorted by coordinate to produce final cleaned BAM files for downstream analysis. BAM indices were generated using samtools index. Peaks were called using MACS2 (v2.2.9.1)135. The effective genome size (-g) was set to 4.2 Gb, approximating the size of the barley genome. Peaks were called with automatic threshold evaluation (–cutoff-analysis), and all duplicate reads were retained during the analysis to preserve biological signal.

VRN1 and ZCCT genes were identified in all assembled wild barley genomes using blastn searches (blast-plus/2.12.0)114 with VRN1 MorexV3 (NC_058522.1:c528157887–528147799) and NCBI GenBank ZCCTa/b/c queries (AY485977, AY485978 and AY687931). Corresponding regions were extracted from genome assemblies by bedtools (v2.26.0)69 and manually annotated and analysed by Geneious Prime software (v2024.0.5; https://www.geneious.com). Sequence similarity visualization of the 2 kb region upstream of the transcription start site and the first intron of VRN1 genes was done by flexidot (v1.06)136. The 79-bp deletion in H. cordobense and H. muticum VRN1 gene was detected by MSA of the extracted VRN1 sequences from wild Hordeum species and winter cultivar Igri in Geneious Prime software (v2023.0.4; https://www.geneious.com) with MAFFT101. The critical region of cultivar Igri was identified in a previous study51.

Sources indicate that three biological replicates were analysed for each stage (14 DAG, 28 DAG) of H. cordobense and H. californicum grown under controlled non-vernalizing conditions (21 °C day:18 °C night, 14 h light:10 h dark photoperiod). Total RNA was extracted from frozen leaf tissue using a Quick-RNA Miniprep Kit (Zymo Research). RNA quality and concentration were evaluated with a Bioanalyzer 2100 (Agilent Technologies) on RNA 6000 Nano chips (Agilent Technologies). H. cordobense 28 DAG RNA-seq libraries and small RNA-seq libraries were constructed according to Illumina instructions and sequenced on a NovaSeq 6000 platform at Novogene. Other sequencing libraries (H. cordobense 14 DAG and H. californicum 14 and 28 DAG; small RNA and RNA-seq) were constructed at the Institute of Experimental Botany (Olomouc) using NEBNext Multiplex Small RNA Library Prep Set for Illumina and NEBNext Ultra RNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina with poly-A selection and sequenced on Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform, 150 PE mode.

According to recent reports, small RNA-seq read trimming and sequencing adaptor removal were done with cutadapt (v3.4)137. Only reads of length 21–24 nt were used for subsequent analyses. ShortStack (v4)138 was used to map small RNA reads to the corresponding genome with default parameters. Bigwig files were created from bam files in a combination of samtools (v1.11)67 and deepTools (v3.5.6)139 with parameters bigwigAverage, bamCoverage–binSize 10,–normalizeUsing BPM. Visualization of small RNA and mRNA bigwig files were done with pyGenomeTracks (v3.9)140.

RNA-seq read trimming on quality (Q30) and sequencing adaptor removal were done with Trimmomatic (v0.32)126. Resulting high-quality reads from each library were mapped onto the corresponding reference genome using STAR (v2.7.7a)127, with default parameters. Mapped reads quantification was done by rsem (v1.3.3)141.

Ten seeds per each of 14 selected Hordeum species accessions (BCC 2067 H. cordobense, BCC 2058 H. californicum, BCC 2014 H. muticum, BCC 2055 H. jubatum, BCC 2001 H. marinum, BCC 2009 H. murinum subsp. murinum, BCC 2017 H. murinum subsp. glaucum, BCC 2023 H. flexuosum, BCC 2026 H. erectifolium, BCC 2028 H. pubiflorum, BCC 2043 H. pusillum, BCC 2059 H. intercedens, BCC 2065 H. patagonicum and BCC 2069 H. roshevitzii) were used. Spring cultivated barley genotypes Morex and Golden Promise and winter genotypes Igri and Antonella were included as controls and were treated identically to wild species. Seeds were stratified at 4 °C for 4 days, germinated in Petri dishes on moist filter paper and then transferred to soil. Plants were grown under controlled non-vernalizing conditions (21 °C day:18 °C night, 14 h light:10 h dark photoperiod) in a growth chamber and cultivated until senescence. Days to flowering were scored in three-day intervals, and the plants were considered flowering at the first emergence of the awn tips. Plants were imaged using a Nikon D5600 digital camera.

Recent findings suggest that the elongated outer glume 1 (eog1) mutants from cultivated barley59, including eog1.a (GSHO 1891), eog1.c (GSHO 1892), eog1.e (GSHO 285) and macrolepis (lep-e.1; GSHO 960), were obtained from the Barley Genetic Stock Collection. Several mutants, namely M2342, M9630, M9815 and M11405, were identified from independent M2 lines of the previously established barley HTX mutagenesis population142. SEM observations were conducted using a Hitachi SEM SU8081 following a standard protocol143. Young inflorescences were sampled and examined. Allelism test was performed by crossing M9630 with GSHO 1891 and GSHO 1892, respectively. All F1 progeny exhibited elongated glumes on the central fertile spikelet (Extended Data Fig. 12d). Sequence-specific amplification of the C2H2-zinc-finger transcription factor gene was performed using primers T-70820-F (5′-TAGGACCGCATATTTCCAGG-3′) and T-70820-R (5′-GAACAGTTCCAAGGCGAAAG-3′). The resulting amplicons were sequenced using Sanger sequencing.

Clean reads (Supplementary Table 20) were obtained by removing the adapters, reads containing N bases and low-quality reads using fastp (v0.20.1) with default parameters144. Clean reads were mapped to their respective reference genomes via Hisat2 v2.1.0 with default parameters145. Read counts were determined from the mapping files via featureCounts (v2.0.1) using standard parameters128, and the TPM values of each gene were calculated. Spike-specific expressed genes were defined as having less than 5% TPM in other tissues146. The heatmap was generated using the pheatmap R package (https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=pheatmap) based on the normalized TPM values. Venn diagrams were drawn using the eulerr package (v6.1.0; https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=eulerr). A local BLAST search was performed using the deduced amino acids of HORVU.MOREX.r3.2HG0170820.1 (EOG1) as the query against the 24 Hordeum genome sequences to identify homologous proteins. Amino acid sequence alignment was carried out using MUSCLE (v3.8)115, and the resulting MSA was visualized with the Simple MSA Viewer function of TBtools II147.

All sequence data generated in this study have been deposited at the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA) under umbrella BioProject PRJEB128330. Accession codes for individual accessions are listed in Supplementary Table 3 (genome sequencing) and Supplementary Table 6 (transcriptome sequencing). The assemblies and annotations are available for download from the IPK Galaxy server (https://galaxy-web.ipk-gatersleben.de/libraries). Gene and TE annotations, MSAs and coordinates of conserved regions have been deposited at the Plant Genomics and Phenomics Research Data Repository148 (https://doi.org/10.5447/ipk/2026/11). The pangenome graph in GFA format has been deposited in the Plant Genomics and Phenomics Research Data Repository148 (https://doi.org/10.5447/ipk/2025/12).

Code for gene annotation, pangenomic analyses and graph construction is available at GitHub (https://github.com/PGSB-HMGU/BPGv2, https://github.com/jia-wu-feng/Pan_Hordeum and https://github.com/cropgeeks/panHordeum).

Bar chart illustrating the number of genes shared between different combinations of accessions within the Hordeum pangenome. (c) Bar chart illustrating the proportion of genes contained in the core-, shell-, and cloud- gene portions by individual accessions.

It has been revealed that (a) NLR gene copy numbers across 34 Hordeum haplomes. The central line in each boxplot represents the median; the box spans the interquartile range (IQR), and whiskers extend to 1.5 × IQR. TNL: Contain TIR, NBS, and LRR domains. CNL: Contain CC, NBS, and LRR domains. RNL: Contain RPW8, NBS, and LRR domains. RN: Contain RPW8 and NBS domains only. NL: Contain NBS and LRR domains, but lack TIR, CC, and RPW8. TN: Contain TIR and NBS domains only. CN: Contain CC and NBS domains only. NBS-only: Contain only the NBS domain. TIR = Toll/Interleukin-1 Receptor-like; NBS = Nucleotide-Binding Site; LRR = Leucine-Rich Repeat; CC = Coiled-Coil; RPW8 = Resistance to Powdery Mildew 8-like domain. (b) Comparison of NLR copy numbers among Hordeum genomes. Welch’s t-test revealed a highly significant difference between the I genome group and other genome groups (two-sided Welch’s t-test, P = 1.8 × 10−6). (c) Bar chart showing the number of accessions represented in each NLR orthogroup (OG). The x-axis indicates accession count per OG. The pie chart summarizes conserved vs. variable genes across 27 accessions. (d) Distribution of NLR gene clusters (≥3 genes) across 34 haplomes. Dot size represents the number of genes per cluster. The chr4H/chr5H group showed significantly different values compared to other chromosomes (two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test, P < 2.2 × 10−16).

(a) Schematic overview of the hybridization scanning method. (b) Density distribution of normalized Robinson–Foulds (nRF) distances. The red line (nRF = 0.21) represents the empirical threshold separating the two peaks corresponding to background phylogenetic variation and regions with elevated phylogenetic discordance. (c) Distribution of normalized Robinson–Foulds (nRF) distances between local gene trees and the species-wide reference tree across the genome. Horizontal line segments indicate the genomic intervals spanned by genes included in each local tree, whereas points mark the midpoint of each interval. The y-axis highlights the nRF distance between each local tree and the reference tree, quantifying their topological dissimilarity. Orange indicates nRF values > 0.21, whereas light blue indicates values ≤ 0.21. (d) Comparative analysis of chromosome 5H between H. jubatum and its ancestral diploid genomes. Orange lines indicate regions with duplications and deletions. A total of n = 128, 178, 164, 142, 144, 118 and 142 local trees were analyzed for chr1H-chr7H, respectively. (e) Local phylogenetic analysis of the segmental exchange region on chromosome 5H (523,129,800–584,948,519 bp). The phylogenetic tree was reconstructed using concatenated single-copy genes located within this region, with bootstrap values shown at each node. Red branches indicate topological changes relative to the genome-wide reference species tree. The local phylogeny revealed segmental exchanges between the two subgenomes of the allotetraploid H. gussoneanum BCC2005 and between the two subgenomes of the allotetraploid H. jubatum. An Approximately Unbiased (AU) test supported the local phylogenetic topology (p-AU = 1.0) and rejected the genome-wide reference topology (p-AU = 2.11 × 10−84). (f) Local phylogenetic analysis of the segmental exchange region on chromosome 4H (495,575,039–607,499,705 bp), performed using the same approach as in (e). The local phylogeny revealed segmental exchanges between the two subgenomes of the allotetraploid H. jubatum and between subgenomes 2 and 3 of the allohexaploid H. parodii. An AU test supported the local phylogenetic topology (p-AU = 1.0) and rejected the genome-wide reference topology (p-AU = 6.55 × 10−57).

Real Madrid attacker agrees contract until 2031 despite starting just twice under Mourinho

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (811 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Naim Beneddra | 20 Nov 2026 15:39.
  • Real Madrid are reportedly preparing to secure the future of an out-of-favour attacker with an extraordinary £880m release clause, despite his limited involvement under Jose Mourinho this season.
  • Morocco international Brahim Diaz is remarked to have agreed a new contract until June 2031, potentially extending his stay at the Santiago Bernabeu by another four years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Naim Beneddra | 20 Nov 2026 15:39.

Real Madrid are reportedly preparing to secure the future of an out-of-favour attacker with an extraordinary £880m release clause, despite his limited involvement under Jose Mourinho this season.

Morocco international Brahim Diaz is remarked to have agreed a new contract until June 2031, potentially extending his stay at the Santiago Bernabeu by another four years.

According to Spanish television programme El Chiringuito, the agreement includes a €1bn (£880m) release clause, with an official announcement expected next week.

Journalist Marcos Benito claims the 27-year-old signed the extension approximately two weeks ago, although Madrid have yet to confirm the arrangement publicly.

The reported deal is particularly striking given Brahim's position in Mourinho's squad, where he has struggled to secure regular opportunities despite contributing three assists this season.

His long-term future may be approaching a resolution, but his immediate prospects of becoming a first-team regular appear considerably less certain.

Brahim's existing agreement is due to expire in June 2027, making his future a subject of considerable speculation during the opening months of the campaign.

Real Madrid have been working to retain the versatile attacker, who returned from a three-year loan spell at AC Milan in 2023 and has provided valuable attacking depth in recent seasons.

However, he has found opportunities increasingly difficult to secure since Mourinho took charge.

The former Manchester City youngster has made nine appearances across all competitions in 2026-27, starting only twice and accumulating just 249 minutes of playing time.

His average of fewer than 28 minutes per appearance underlines the limited nature of his involvement, while he has started the last 11 matches on the bench.

Brahim has nevertheless contributed three assists, demonstrating that he can still influence matches during relatively brief appearances.

Competition for attacking positions has become particularly demanding.

Arda Guler has established himself as a more prominent member of Mourinho's plans, while Jude Bellingham and summer signing Yan Diomande occupy crucial roles in Madrid's attacking structure.

Vinicius Junior's anticipated return from suspension and Rodrygo's recovery from injury could further complicate Brahim's attempts to secure additional minutes.

The situation has already prompted questions about his future.

Earlier this month, Sports Mole reported on Brahim's prolonged spell among the substitutes and the growing concerns surrounding his lack of playing time.

Despite those difficulties, Mourinho has reportedly supported the club's efforts to retain the Morocco international.

The proposed extension would strengthen Madrid's contractual position considerably, although a release clause of €1bn should not be interpreted as a realistic valuation or asking price.

Such figures are frequently included in contracts at major Spanish clubs to provide protection against unwanted departures.

There is, however, some uncertainty surrounding the precise duration of Brahim's latest deal.

While El Chiringuito reports an agreement until 2031, Spanish newspaper AS has suggested that his renewal is arranged until 2030.

Neither version has been officially confirmed by Real Madrid.

Securing a latest contract would represent a significant commitment from Madrid, but it would not guarantee Brahim a more substantial role in the team.

His position is particularly intriguing given that the club have several established attacking options and continue to develop younger players competing for similar positions.

For Brahim, the challenge is to turn occasional contributions into a more consistent place in Mourinho's starting XI.

That question also has implications for Morocco, where the midfielder remains an crucial international despite his restricted opportunities in Spain.

The Atlas Lions are building towards the 2030 World Cup, which Morocco will co-host alongside Spain and Portugal.

National team coach Mohamed Ouahbi has previously expressed a desire to see his players become more influential at club level, while acknowledging Brahim's ability to make a difference for his country.

Former Morocco international Mustapha Hadji has taken a stronger position, publicly questioning whether such limited club involvement is compatible with regular international selection.

Brahim's reported extension therefore raises an obvious sporting dilemma.

Remaining at the Bernabeu offers the prospect of competing for major trophies and retaining his place at one of Europe's most prestigious clubs.

However, the attacking competition that has restricted him to just two starts this season is unlikely to disappear simply because his contractual future is secured.

The deal would also make a potential departure more complicated, with interested clubs likely to require negotiations with Madrid rather than having the opportunity to sign him as a free agent next summer.

There is no indication that Brahim has asked to leave, and his reported decision to extend his contract suggests that he remains committed to fighting for his place.

For Mourinho, the challenge is different: finding sufficient opportunities for a talented squad player whom Madrid appear determined to retain for the long term.

An official announcement could settle the uncertainty surrounding Brahim's contract, but his limited involvement on the pitch remains a separate issue that the new agreement cannot resolve.

When Manchester City play like this what a loss their football will be to the Premier League – and the Champions League – if they are heavily sanctioned later this season.

Industry observers note that in what turned out to be a match for the ages, a night of brilliant, unbridled attack, we were treated to the ultimate game of two halves as the back-to-back European champions Paris St-Germain took City apart for 45 minutes. And then were left holding on.

According to recent reports, city will hope this is a sign of what is to come in their Premier League fight. But with a different result. After suffering a resounding defeat at the hands of the Premier League’s independent commission, with 114 of the 115 charges against them proven, they maintain their innocence and are mounting an appeal.

Could they make a comeback? It would be incredible and highly improbable if they did so but, out on the pitch, and 3-0 down after a first half in which they were in danger of being humiliated by PSG, they created enough opportunities to save themselves.

The data backed that. City’s expected goals (xG) was 2.57 while PSG’s was 1.83. City had 27 shots to 15 and had more possession and more passes. Enzo Maresca made a triple substitution to devastating effect, especially with the introduction of new signings Ayyoub Bouaddi and Iliman Ndiaye.

In the end they clawed back two goals, both scored by Erling Haaland, who now has 61 in 60 games in this competition – seventh outright in the all-time list, before Ruud van Nistelrooy. And 37 of those for City, overtaking Sergio Agüero’s club record.

Erling Haaland gets his second of the night, and the game could be back on 🔥 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/sFZ0eT2Egz.

It could have been a hat-trick. It could even have been four as Haaland, taking the captain’s armband as Rúben Dias was withdrawn during the interval, clipped the top of the crossbar with a header and then was denied by goalkeeper Matvei Safonov as the striker slid in.

“Even with 3-0 in the first half, with the amount of chances we created in the second half, we deserved more. Luis [Enrique, PSG’s coach] noted at the end of the game that they were quite lucky,” Maresca claimed before being asked whether he would relish facing PSG again, later in this competition. “My feeling is we are there. We are close,” he added.

Did City deserve a draw? No one was predicting that at half-time as they were suffering as comprehensive a defeat as was inflicted by the commission. Accused of “sham” contracts to inflate income, this was a sham of a performance, made all the more emphatic because of how brilliant PSG, and their exceptional 21-year-old winger Désiré Doué, were.

The question, also, was: would the eighth meeting of these clubs in the Champions League in the last 11 seasons be the last for some time?

After Manchester City’s conviction by an independent commission on 114 charges of financial malpractice in contravention of Premier League rules, finding the right tone to use to cover their matches during their appeal is difficult. While they are in limbo, the rest of English football is in purgatory and although Gary Neville, the Pope of Pilsworth, in unsurprisingly hyperbolic fashion has mentioned he would prefer not to cover City’s games in future, that is not an indulgence a serious news organisation would countenance. They have to be covered and the concerns addressed.

Having said that, in this format of a rolling report on the old minute-by-minute template, I think we have to cover the controversy and its implications in the whole during the build-up and keep an eye on reaction and references to it during the run of play. But I don’t think it would serve anyone to take the stance during the live coverage that anything that is happening on the field is unimportant, redundant and ultimately void because of the guilty verdicts, and hence adopt a flippant tone. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

And if Leeds United are performing and carrying themselves like an established Premier League team, perhaps it is time to start treating them as one.

A growing number of pundits are viewing Leeds in those terms after being impressed by the way the club have taken to life back in the top flight.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

United's physicality and intensity have marked them out as one of the hardest teams to beat. They have lost just seven league games since the start of 2026, while their defence ranks among the best in the division this season – an improvement underpinned by summer signings James Trafford and Tarik Muharemovic.

Farke himself feels his players have done enough to earn the respect of pundits, although he has cautioned them against believing the hype.

Recent findings suggest that "It's a credit to our work in the last years," he said. "I would also agree, based on our performances, that we deserve a bit the label and praise.

"But we also don't go into the trap where we think that we are already the finished product or better than we are. We know that we have to fight for each and every point because other clubs are more established.

In a recent development, "We have an unbelievable tradition and are a huge club in the UK. Everyone knows that this club belongs at the top level.

In a recent development, "We have a clear vision for our short, mid-term and long-term but it's also fair to say that in the last 25 years we haven't spent too many years at the Premier League level. Our best finish in that time is exactly one top-half finish in position nine.

"For that, we don't go into the trap and believe all the praise. We know that we are good and are not doubting ourselves too much; we play with confidence.

In a recent development, "But we don't go into the trap of thinking that we can win games with even 95 per cent effort. We're still a side in our second year after promotion and have to show some craft and fight in order to become an established Premier League side.".

Chelsea provide another measure of Leeds' progress today, the first of three challenging away assignments before Christmas.

Farke, whose side travel to Manchester City and Liverpool in early December, is bidding to become the first United manager to mastermind a win at Stamford Bridge since David O'Leary in 1999.

"I know it's a while ago since we travelled away from Stamford Bridge with three points," said Farke.

It has been revealed that "It will be difficult but if we are at our very best, we also know we're capable of winning points wherever we go. We have to make sure we are on it.

In a recent development, "The preparations have been difficult this week but it's also very similar for Chelsea. We're looking forward to this game.".

Leeds return from the international break hoping to build on their impressive victory over in-form Tottenham Hotspur.

Chelsea, meanwhile, are looking to respond to their disappointing defeat at Sunderland last time out.

Xabi Alonso's side have shown their attacking potential in flashes – not least when they hammered Leeds 6-3 in the League Cup – but a record of five wins, four defeats and a solitary draw in the league hints at a team still finding their way under the latest manager.

Farke, however, has warned his players not to read too much into Chelsea's inconsistency.

"I expect top-class players and also a top manager," he said.

Recent findings suggest that "It's no secret that they have world-class potential in their squad. That's why they've spent so much money in the last years – to build a squad with unbelievable individual quality, especially up front.

"It's difficult. It's never guaranteed that if you have so many quality players that you play each and every opponent out of the park.

"Some of their last opponents have made their life difficult but it's still crucial to be aware of their quality and strength. We have to make sure we don't allow them to develop that strength.

"It's also notable that we take part in this game in terms of having as much possession as possible and that we also dominate the ball because when they have the ball, they have so much talent, skill and potential to make something happen.

It has been revealed that "For Leeds United, it's always a bit of a special fixture to travel to London and play Chelsea. We are very respectful but definitely not fearful.".

Leeds took four points off the Blues last season on their way to a 14th-place finish.

They have made an encouraging start to their second campaign back at the top level but Farke is staying grounded.

The Leeds boss expects the coming weeks to offer a clearer indication of how the table is shaping up as clubs brace themselves for a long, uninterrupted run of fixtures.

"Until November, it's the starting period of the Premier League," said Farke. "It's vital to put yourselves into a good position. We have done this with good performances and are sitting on 14 points in the top half of the table.

"There will be many, many games and challenges due to workloads, injuries, illnesses and perhaps suspensions. For that, it's not the moment to be too carried away. It's a period where we have to be really on it and fight for everything.

"After this period, we can have a look and see where we are in the table for the run-in. This upcoming month is quite important for the final table.".

By Darren Plant | 20 Nov 2026 16:12.

Unai Emery has confirmed that Matty Cash is one of three Aston Villa players who will miss Saturday's Premier League fixture against Sunderland.

Despite the Spaniard receiving rave reviews in recent months, Villa return from the November international break on a four-match winless streak.

Twice giving up a two-goal lead at Manchester United in their most recent game has left Villa in 10th place in the Premier League table.

With a Champions League showdown at Galatasaray to come on Tuesday, Emery must find a balance when naming his starting lineup for the game with the Black Cats.

Speaking at a press conference on Friday, Emery revealed that Cash would not be available.

While on international duty with Poland, Cash suffered a concussion during the fixture with Romania.

Meanwhile, Matteo Ruggeri and Amadou Onana - who signed a latest contract earlier this week - are also missing.

Emery told reporters: "The players, more or less, they are good. Not so many changes with the players [out] injured.

"Of course, [Matty] Cash is [out with] concussion and Amadou Onana and Matteo Ruggeri they are both still out.

"Other players - they are ready.".

Although there was no mention of Aaron Wan-Bissaka after his recent injury, the expectation is that the Congo DR right-back will deputise for Cash.

Despite their exit from the EFL Cup, Villa still face a schedule that sees them playing seven times between November 21 and December 13.

Following the Sunderland and Galatasaray double-header, the West Midlands outfit play Ipswich Town, Everton, Crystal Palace, Paris Saint-Germain and Coventry City.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 15:24 EST, 19 November 2026 | Updated: 16:32 EST, 19 November 2026.

Blackpool have sacked manager Ian Evatt just hours after wishing him a happy birthday.

Evatt had been in charge for a year and his final match was Saturday's 1-0 away defeat by fellow strugglers AFC Wimbledon, when his squad was decimated by illness. The result left the Seasiders immediately above the League One relegation zone and followed a run of one win and six defeats in ten league games.

Blackpool’s social media team had earlier wished Evatt a happy 45th birthday with the pay-off line: 'Have a great day, Gaffer!'.

Three hours later, Evatt was relieved of his duties, and the club began the search for their ninth manager in eight years.

Evatt’s contract was set to run until June 2028. He joined last October following his exit from Bolton Wanderers in January 2025.

Blackpool later thanked the 45-year-old for his efforts during his time with the club.

Blackpool sacked manager Ian Evatt just hours after wishing him a happy 45th birthday.

Blackpool posted the birthday message just after 9am in the morning, with Evatt's sacking then confirmed at 4pm.

Former Crystal Palace chairman Simon Jordan famously claimed to have sacked Trevor Francis on his birthday back in 2003.

Francis' dismissal has become an often told tale, with Jordan writing sixteen years after the event that he had even offered to send the former England star a birthday card.

Recent reports have also involved the suggestion that Francis had mumbled 'but its my birthday' back to Jordan when he was given his marching orders.

Whether these events played out as told are unclear. But Crystal Palace officially announced Francis' departure on April 18 in 2003, with his birthday falling a day later.

Industry observers note that 'I am totally committed to playing in the Premier League and I will ensure the latest manager can achieve this aspiration,' Jordan wrote on Crystal Palace's website at the time. 'I would like to thank Trevor for all his hard work and would like to wish him the very best for the future.'.

Sources indicate that jordan then turned on the players, adding: 'I'm not watching next year what I've had to watch this year. At times we've been a disgrace.

'I've asked the management staff to tell me who should go. They can see the players who are performing and those who are not and you will see in the summer, out they will go. The players will be told when it suits me. I care about them as much they care about me.'.

Francis had reportedly told his players in a parting shot: 'Well, lads, I've been sacked – have a good summer holiday.'.

Palace appointed Steve Kember as manager in the summer and despite Jordan's hopes of automatic promotion, rather than the play-offs, found themselves in a relegation battle in November.

Iain Dowie was appointed as manager the following month and guided Palace into the play-offs, with the Eagles triumphing in Cardiff to secure promotion to the top flight.

Steve Thompson will step in to take charge of the team against Wigan Athletic this weekend, his fourth spell as caretaker, alongside Stephen Crainey, Stephen Dobbie and Steve Banks.

Industry observers note that during a hugely successful playing career at Bloomfield Road, Evatt made over 250 appearances for Blackpool. In his six years at the club, he played a vital role in their rise from League One to the Premier League, which included two successful play-off campaigns.

On arrival as a manager, he amassed 13 points from a possible 15 in December 2025 to lift them out of the relegation zone, although they lost ten and won two of their next 15 matches in all competitions.

They finished the campaign strongly, with six wins in seven games as part of a sequence of one defeat in 13 between mid-March and the end of August, only to struggle again this season.

At Manchester Magistrates’ Court, the 30-year-old pleaded not guilty to using threatening, abusive or insulting behaviour with intent to cause fear of, or provoke, unlawful violence.

He is alleged to have punched a Rochdale fan during a pitch invasion that took place when the two sides met in the National League on April 25.

York have offered their support to Boateng, who has been training ahead of Walsall’s visit tomorrow (November 21).

Recent findings suggest that “I haven’t had to [put an arm around Hiram],” noted Lindsey, as reported by York Press. “I probably have subconsciously.

“I have spoken to him and he’s in a good place, he’s playing some really good football at the moment and is getting back up to speed playing some football after being out for a while.

“What was pleasing was when we were looking to bring him off around the 60 minute mark [against Rochdale], he was okay to stay on.

“He did get a little bit of a knock just before he came off, but he’s okay.".

Boateng is charged with a section four public order offence that carries a maximum sentence of six months in prison.

A spokesperson for York remarked Boateng “maintains the full support of everyone at York City and is a much-valued member of the squad, both on and off the pitch”.

The ex-Crystal Palace man missed the early stages of the season through injury but has appeared in four of York’s last five League Two games.

According to recent reports, “He’s playing some good football at the moment,” said Lindsey. “I think that his focus is on the football, which it needs to be.

“For all of the time that things are going on in the background, you’ve got to focus on something that’s good, and that’s good in his life at the moment.

“We need to continue doing that.”.

Fourth-placed York could break into the automatic promotion places in League Two with a win over sixth-placed Walsall, who trail the Minstermen by just one point.

Without being picture-perfect, United are well-placed just outside of the top eight ahead of today's resumption of business, with United starting out with a Bramall Lane double-header against former club Watford and the club where he started out in football, Southampton.

A third of the way into the campaign, just eight points separate current leaders Birmingham City from 13th-placed Blackburn Rovers. Plenty can happen - and will - between now and January 1.

Wilder mentioned: "I've got to say, I don't think there is a Leeds United, Burnley and Sheffield United situation this year (like in 2024-25).

In a recent development, "It wasn't last year. Coventry were obviously the standout team. Everybody tipped Ipswich at the start of the season and they took the time to get going.

"That's the nature of the division. Everybody's looking for that consistency and it's been that rollercoaster ride for everybody (so far). We've had to endure it and suffer it as well.

According to recent reports, "We've enjoyed some good wins as well, but I think we're all after that consistency. I'm looking for us, off an average start and a better last nine games, to push on into January and then to kick on into the second part of the season.".

Behind-the-scenes, this period is also critical for instigating plans for the winter window.

Should further incremental progress in results dovetail with a strong mid-season window, then the Blades will be a team to watch in the new year.

If remains a major if, more especially with the well-documented off-the-field situation at the club.

Industry observers note that on his transfer budget, Wilder continued: "That's fluid and that'll be in conversations with the owners. But the (recruitment) guys have been working right the way through since the last window.

According to recent reports, "I've got an idea what I need. It's not four, five and six, but I do think we might need a little bit of help and a bit of a push with a couple of players coming in.

"We've got a loan slot available. The landscape's changed a little bit now with Femi, but I think we can cover that.

"It'll be two or three with my recommendations to push on and make us better and hopefully give us the opportunity of extending our season.".

Seriki has had an operation after rupturing his patella tendon in the recent game at Charlton Athletic - with the 'devastated' right-back/wing-back sidelined for the next 12 months.

Wilder added: "We're devastated for him because this is a big injury for him. One hundred per cent, he will make a full recovery.

Manchester United manager Mauricio Pochettino could recall Lisandro Martinez to his starting lineup for his opening game in charge away to Liverpool on Sunday in the Premier League.

The Argentine defender is available to his compatriot after completing a domestic suspension and could now slot back into the rearguard alongside Harry Maguire, who has seemingly shaken off a back problem.

Noussair Mazraoui would be the most likely to make way if Martinez returns, as Leny Yoro shuffles over to right-back, on the opposite side to the much-maligned Diogo Dalot.

The Portugal international's withdrawal was cheered by fans in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa, but with Patrick Dorgu operating in a more attack-minded role of late and Luke Shaw still doubtful, Dalot should reprise his role.

The same goes for Youri Tielemans and Kobbie Mainoo in the middle, as Pochettino sticks to a 4-2-3-1 setup for his maiden match and forces Andrey Santos to wait his turn.

The front four of Amad Diallo, Bruno Fernandes, Matheus Cunha and Bryan Mbeumo is likely to remain the same too, although Marcus Rashford (hip) is on the verge of returning and could be an option on Merseyside.

Carlos Baleba (hamstring), Manuel Ugarte (knee) and Benjamin Sesko (calf) all remain out of contention for the away side.

Manchester United possible starting lineup:.

Lammens; Yoro, Martinez, Maguire, Dalot; Tielemans, Mainoo; Diallo, Fernandes, Cunha; Mbeumo.

💡 Key Takeaways
